Jason Green, commander of the 120th Airlift Wing, serves as an aircraft commander during the Montana Air National Guard’s final tactical training flight with the C-130H Hercules over Montana, Oct. 3, 2026. The two-ship tactical formation marked the close of the wing’s 12-year C-130H mission, which began after the 120th transitioned from fighter aircraft to tactical airlift in 2013. Green participated in the historic flight as the wing concluded tactical training with the H-mo
items.body:
Jason Green, commander of the 120th Airlift Wing, serves as an aircraft commander during the Montana Air National Guard’s final tactical training flight with the C-130H Hercules over Montana, Oct.

The two-ship tactical formation marked the close of the wing’s 12-year C-130H mission, which began after the 120th transitioned from fighter aircraft to tactical airlift in 2013.

Green participated in the historic flight as the wing concluded tactical training with the H-model and prepared for its transition to the C-130J Super Hercules.

The remaining C-130Hs are scheduled to depart Great Falls by the end of October, while the wing’s first C-130J is expected to arrive in 2027.

items.title: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
items.author: Mohammed Ghobari, Timour Azhari and Eman Abouhassira, Reuters
items.summary: Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.
items.body:
Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.

The government’s armed forces would press the offensive “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia,” Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address. A military spokesman later called on the Houthis to lay down their weapons.

The Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, have held Yemen’s capital Sanaa and vast parts of the northwest, where most of the population live, since 2014. They have so far withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies, and have updated their weaponry with the help of Iran.

The movement launched a surprise offensive last month which captured the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and some 90 miles of coast on the Red Sea in a matter of weeks, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route.

That advance also opened a new front in the wider U.S.-Israeli war launched in February against Iran, to which Tehran’s responses included choking oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, to the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

HOUTHIS SAY THEY STRUCK SAUDI ARABIA

As the Yemeni government, known as the Presidential Leadership Council, made its announcement, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia.

They claimed the attacks caused major fires and were in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.

Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict had been exhausted.

He thanked Saudi Arabia for its support and called on Yemen’s regional allies and international partners to support PLC forces and institutions.

Regional and Western officials told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.

NEW FRONT IN MIDEAST WAR

The U.S. is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh’s operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters.

The United States’ war on Iran has decimated a layer of Iranian military and political leadership, but has also entangled Washington in a new engagement in the Middle East and depleted crucial military hardware.

Yemen has been mired in conflict for years, with an array of local armed groups and factions backed by competing regional and international actors.

After a popular uprising that was part of the Arab Spring movements in 2011, the Houthis, an armed group of Zaidi Shi’ite Muslims, captured Sanaa.

The Saudi-backed PLC, which is also recognized by the United Nations, has, since the Houthi takeover, controlled the south and east of the country, based in the former South Yemen capital of Aden.

Saudi Arabia entered Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the PLC, but failed to defeat the Houthis.

A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

The Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground since seizing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in their lightning offensive last month that saw government forces collapse.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen’s Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden on the southern coast.

Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen’s third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.

The city is important not just for its strategic location; Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.

Three in four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

items.title: The Backbone Behind the Mission: ADP Keeps TR Connected
items.author: SN Devin Kraemer
items.summary: Aboard USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71), nearly every Sailor depends on computers, networks, and digital systems to carry out daily operations. The Automated Data processing (ADP) division is responsible for delivering and maintaining the technology that enables the crew to communicate, coordinate, and execute the mission.
items.body: Aboard USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71), nearly every Sailor depends on computers, networks, and digital systems to carry out daily operations. The Automated Data processing (ADP) division is responsible for delivering and maintaining the technology that enables the crew to communicate, coordinate, and execute the mission. ADP Sailors respond to technical issues across every deck and workspace, tracking down trouble tickets wherever they arise. Their responsibilities range from resolving network connectivity and hardware failures to securing databases, ensuring that every Sailor has reliable access to the systems required for mission success. “We maintain extremely important aspects of the mission everywhere we go” said Chief Information Systems Technician Timothy Highland. “Not only every system we rely on when using the CANES computers, but we also allow the destroyers to connect to our targeting programs while they launch missiles and track any that are incoming.” ADP maintains the ship’s networks that support daily operations, from individual computer accounts and email to maintenance tracking and scheduling systems. Both Non-classified Internet Protocol Router (NIPR) and Secret Internet Protocol Router (SIPR) applications rely on these networks. Through ongoing training in software troubleshooting and hardware repair, ADP enables the crew to focus on their duties without interruption from technical problems. For the ADP Sailors, the work extends beyond technical repairs. Each call brings them into contact with shipmates from every department, allowing them to resolve issues that directly impact daily life and mission readiness. “You get to go around the ship, talk to people and help a lot of people every day,” said Information Systems Technician 3rd Class Tanner Kattke. “My favorite part of the job is making connections while traveling around the ship and helping people.” The pace is constant, with requests coming from every corner of the ship. For the ADP team, the reward is seeing Sailors return to their duties. Their work often goes unseen when systems run smoothly, but when a network fails or a critical connection is lost, their expertise becomes essential to restoring operations.

items.title: Deployment in the Spotlight
items.author: PO3 Gary Buckles
items.summary: Aviation Boatswain’s Mate Airman (Equipment) Angelee Rosales and Chief Aviation Boatswain’s Mate (Handling) Michael Cole speak about learning how to live and work as a team far from home.
items.body: For Sailors experiencing their first deployment, leaving home can bring a mixture of anticipation, uncertainty and excitement. The months leading up to deployment are filled with preparations: organizing personal gear, managing finances, arranging vehicle storage and saying goodbye to family and friends. Once underway, however, the focus shifts from preparing to deploy to learning how to live and work as a team far from home. For Aviation Boatswain’s Mate Airman (Equipment) Angelee Rosales, assigned to the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) Air Department, her first deployment is an opportunity to embrace the challenges ahead while helping the Sailors around her do the same. “I just want to be positive and uplifting for everyone in my department,” said Rosales. “We get a lot of really young people in our department and we pretty much just have each other out there with how busy our work schedule is with the air wing onboard, so it’s a lot like a very big family outside of your actual family.” Rosales is also using the deployment to pursue professional goals. She is working toward qualifying as a shooter, a flight deck position responsible for launching aircraft from the carrier. The qualification carries significant responsibility and represents another step in her development as a Sailor. For Rosales, however, success during deployment is about more than qualifications. She wants to return home with experiences that demonstrate to her family that she remained resilient, even when circumstances became difficult. “I want to be able to tell them about how when we got extended, I didn’t let it get to me,” said Rosales. “I want them to know I wasn’t a quitter.” While Rosales is experiencing her first deployment, Theodore Roosevelt’s crew also includes Sailors who have learned through years of service that the challenges of deployment are easier to navigate when Sailors rely on one another. Chief Aviation Boatswain’s Mate (Handling) Michael Cole, who recently advanced to chief petty officer, understands the importance of maintaining focus while operating far from home. As an experienced Sailor and leader, Cole also recognizes the responsibility that comes with helping junior Sailors navigate their own deployment experiences. “You’ve got to be able to stay true to yourself,” said Cole. “Obviously you’re always going to be thinking about home, but sometimes that can be a distraction to what you do out there, especially if you have one of those high-risk jobs, like myself.” For Sailors working on an aircraft carrier, maintaining that focus is particularly important. The flight deck is a demanding environment where Sailors must communicate effectively, trust their training and rely on the people working beside them. That resilience extends beyond the work itself. Cole said the relationships formed during deployment can become one of the crew’s most important sources of strength, particularly when Sailors are separated from the people they know and love at home. “Deployment tests you, but it also builds something unbreakable,” said Cole. “When you’re thousands of miles from home and communication is cut off, the Sailors standing next to you become your lifeline. You learn to rely on each other for absolutely everything. In the end, they aren't just your crew—they are your family.” For Rosales, that sense of connection is already becoming part of her first deployment experience. From pursuing new qualifications on the flight deck to supporting the Sailors in her department, she is learning what many experienced Sailors already understand: deployment is not defined solely by the miles traveled or time spent away from home. It is defined by the people who make the journey together.

items.title: Lead With a Purpose
items.author: PO1 Storm Henry
items.summary: For a Sailor who began her career as an undesignated Seaman, survived combat and cancer, and rose to senior enlisted leadership aboard an aircraft carrier, Command Master Chief Jackey Smith’s legacy continues to unfold. And the measure of that legacy is clear: ensuring the Sailors who deploy together return home together.
items.body: For Command Master Chief Jackey Smith, leadership is defined by people. It is reflected in Sailors who find the confidence to overcome difficult days, in teammates who trust each other when circumstances turn dangerous, and ultimately, in whether every member of the team returns home together. Smith’s perspective was shaped over a Navy career that began as an undesignated Seaman in the deck department, included combat service in Iraq, a battle with breast cancer and ultimately to her current role as Command Master Chief aboard the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71). Her journey to the Navy began far from the coast. Raised in Nebraska, Smith was pursuing a Marine Corps option through the University of Nebraska’s ROTC program when she decided to change course. After telling her Gunnery Sergeant she intended to enlist, Smith remained determined even after the Marine Corps recruiter could not secure her commitment. The Navy recruiter next door offered her an undesignated Seaman contract and a $3,000 enlistment bonus. Smith accepted. Her first assignment in deck department laid the foundation for her development as a Sailor and leader. “I tell a lot of undesignated Seamen that life in deck is not for the weak,” said Smith. “It’s where you learn your basics of being a Sailor. It’s where you learn the work ethic of making sure that you are pulling your weight on a team. I would never, ever give back that experience.”. Although her supervisor believed she would make a great BM3, Smith had a different goal. She wanted to become a Journalist and pursue a career in public affairs. With the help of her career counselor, Smith struck Journalist and began her public affairs career at Naval Air Station Jacksonville. Unable to attend “A” School, she relied on self-study, learning from rating publications and guidance from her leadership to master the fundamentals and become fully qualified. Her assignments included USS Ashland (LSD 48), Navy Region Mid-Atlantic, and later the Combat Camera detachment in San Diego. At Combat Camera, Smith found herself serving as a Journalist among Photographer’s Mates. Rather than allowing the difference in ratings to limit her role, she sought opportunities to broaden her capabilities. She attended Survival, Evasion, Resistance and Escape school and pursued small-arms qualifications, determined to become a fully qualified member of the team. That training would later become critical. “Utilizing all of that training, once we went into harm’s way, it became second nature to make sure that me and my fellow shipmates and my fellow Army buddies got back to our families,” Smith recalls. Smith deployed to Iraq with a team assigned to search for enemy targets. During one mission, as her team moved through a village, her training became instinctive. “I had the training to know that there was probably a time when I would need to put my camera down and bring my weapon up,” Smith says. That moment arrived when insurgents attacked, triggering an intense firefight. Smith picked up her M4 and returned fire. When the team commander hesitated under threat, she helped refocus the team and led them to the Humvees, returning to the forward operating base. Smith received the Bronze Star for her actions during the firefight. She credits the recognition to the leaders and teammates who invested in training and prepared the team to perform under pressure. In her first eight years, Smith advanced from undesignated Seaman to decorated combat veteran and chief petty officer. She later served as Public Affairs Chief for the Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy, a role she considered the pinnacle of her career. In 2014, Smith’s career took another unexpected turn. Smith was diagnosed with breast cancer and learned the disease was advancing. As a Chief, her instinct was to continue fulfilling her duties and not let cancer interfere with her service. Her Chiefs Mess and leading petty officer saw It differently. They encouraged Smith to take a leave of absence and focus on her health. “At the height of everything, I‘m a faithful person. God said, ‘Hey, slow down. Slow down. Make sure you’re taking care of yourself,’” Smith says. “And taking care of myself meant I needed to be vulnerable.” The experience changed not only Smith’s outlook on life, but also her approach to leadership. Recovering from cancer reinforced for Smith that every Sailor carries a story that may not be visible to those around them. She became more deliberate about understanding the individual behind the uniform and more patient with Sailors as they worked through personal and professional challenges. Smith’s leadership philosophy evolved further during the 2018 Pacific Partnership humanitarian exercise. While she valued supporting Sailors within her rating, the experience showed her the importance of serving the broader team. At her next command, Smith was regularly asked to fill in for the Command Master Chief. These experiences reinforced her commitment to developing Chiefs and supporting Sailors across the command, leading her to pursue the Command Senior Enlisted Leader program. Through the program, Smith served as Command Senior Chief aboard a destroyer and as executive assistant to Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy James Honea. She later became Command Master Chief of Destroyer Squadron 23 before reporting to USS Theodore Roosevelt. Now, as Theodore Roosevelt’s Command Master Chief, Smith emphasizes that the aircraft carrier’s success depends on the entire crew working as one team. She challenges leaders to understand their Sailors, recognize what they need to perform at their best, and help them navigate challenges. She expects junior Sailors to contribute to the team’s success by mastering the basics: arriving on time, wearing the correct uniform, and being ready to work, even when the job is demanding. For Smith, leadership is measured by the team’s ability to succeed together. “I truly believe no-one joined the Navy to fail,” Smith emphatically states. “For the Sailors who think, ‘I’m just doing this,’ or, ‘I only do this,’ my legacy that I wish to have is to allow Sailors to know that whatever it is that they believe that they want to do, they can achieve it. And they can achieve it through hard work. They can achieve it by making sure that whatever mentally is blocking them, they push past it. If I could choose what my legacy on this ship would be, it is making sure that all of our Sailors we deployed with, we came back with.” Smith’s perspective on legacy is rooted in a lesson learned throughout her life: tomorrow is never guaranteed. “People often ask why I’m so happy. It’s simple: I’m a cancer survivor. I survived war in Iraq. And every morning I wake up is another day God has given me. I’ve seen enough in this life to know that tomorrow isn’t promised,” Smith says. “So, when I have been given another day, I’m going to smile, be grateful, love hard, lead with purpose, and make the most of it.” For a Sailor who began her career as an undesignated Seaman, survived combat and cancer, and rose to senior enlisted leadership aboard an aircraft carrier, Smith’s legacy continues to unfold. And the measure of that legacy is clear: ensuring the Sailors who deploy together return home together.

items.title: “Today, Ted Stevens is the fleet”: Secretary of the Navy commissions USS Ted Stevens
items.author: ENS Dylan Barron
items.summary: The U.S. Navy commissioned USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), its third Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, in Whittier, Alaska, honoring Senator Ted Stevens’ legacy while bringing a highly capable warship into active service to defend the homeland, deter aggression and project combat power worldwide.
items.body:
WHITTIER, Alaska (Oct. 3, 2026) — The U.S. Navy placed its newest Flight III Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer, USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), into active commission today during a formal ceremony in Whittier, Alaska.

The commissioning of USS Ted Stevens marks an immediate, decisive leap in naval warfighting readiness and surface fleet lethality. As the second Flight III destroyer to enter active service, USS Ted Stevens provides combatant commanders with unmatched integrated air and missile defense capabilities, directly supporting Department of War priorities to enforce maritime dominance, secure contested sea lanes, and project credible deterrence worldwide.

The ship and its commissioning location honor the legacy of the late Senator Ted Stevens, a decorated combat aviator and lifelong champion for the state of Alaska and the nation's armed forces. Selecting the strategic deep-water port of Whittier highlights Alaska’s enduring maritime significance and the historic partnership between the U.S. Navy and the 49th State. “Woosh-Jee-een,” is a phrase in the southeast Alaskan indigenous language Tlingit meaning “working together” or “pulling together,” which reflects the spirit of partnership between the Navy, the Stevens family, the crew and the people of Alaska.

Senator Stevens served as an Army Air Forces pilot during World War II, flying hazardous transport missions over “The Hump” in the China-Burma-India theater supporting the 14th Air Force “Flying Tigers,” earning two Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals. Returning home after the war, Stevens played an instrumental role in securing Alaska statehood in 1959. During four decades in the U.S. Senate, from 1968 to 2009, he served as President Pro Tempore and President Pro Tempore Emeritus, dedicating his career to modernizing the armed forces, bolstering national security, and ensuring warfighters were equipped to fight and win.

During the ceremony, Acting Secretary of the Navy The Honorable Hung Cao highlighted the significance of the crew’s role in bringing the ship to life as it began its commissioned service.

“Today, USS Ted Stevens is no longer preparing to join the fleet. Today, Ted Stevens is the fleet,” said Cao. “Today, USS Ted Stevens stands ready to defend the homeland, deter aggression, and when called upon, fight and win.”

During the ceremony, the ship’s sponsors, Mrs. Catherine Ann Stevens, wife of Senator Stevens, and his daughters, Mrs. Susan Stevens Covich and Mrs. Lily Stevens Becker, gave the traditional naval order: “Man our ship and bring her to life!” At that command, the commissioning crew ran aboard to man the rails, set the first watch, and bring the warship’s advanced combat systems to full operational status.

“I am deeply honored and proud to be your sponsor, along with my mother and sister Susan,” said Lily Stevens Becker, daughter of Senator Ted Stevens. “As you wake up every day, know that we and every person here believe in you to take care of this ship, take care of each other, and to uphold the peace and safety of our nation.”

The ship's motto, "Lead with Courage," serves as an operational mandate that reflects Senator Stevens’ wartime bravery and channels it into the aggressive combat posture required of today's surface warriors.

“To my crew, my shipmates, the men and women who are the heart and soul of this great ship, you have exceeded all expectations,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Mary Katey Hayes, commanding officer of USS Ted Stevens. “We are ready to answer our nation’s call. We are ready to defend freedom, whether the winds of war blow near the rugged coast of Alaska, or in the far reaches of the globe.”

From the North Pacific campaigns of World War II to modern Arctic maritime operations, the Navy and Alaska share a deep commitment to homeland defense. The commissioning in Whittier emphasizes the Navy’s persistent operational presence in high-latitude environments to deter northern flank aggression and safeguard critical maritime routes.

USS Ted Stevens is built around the AN/SPY-6(V)1 Air and Missile Defense Radar (AMDR) and Aegis Baseline 10 combat system, delivering a generational leap in simultaneous Anti-Air Warfare (AAW) and Ballistic Missile Defense (BMD). Featuring enhanced electrical power distribution and expanded cooling capacity, the destroyer is engineered to operate in high-threat environments and integrate seamlessly with joint and coalition forces.

Following post-commissioning operations, USS Ted Stevens will transit to its permanent homeport in Norfolk, Virginia, fully prepared to deploy worldwide.

The commissioning of the USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128) underscores the Navy's commitment to building America’s Golden Fleet. For 250 years, American naval power has projected strength globally. That mission continues – and intensifies. We operate forward 24/7, 365 days a year. This operational tempo demands continuous capability delivery, and the Golden Fleet is our answer.

Commander, Naval Surface Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet ensures fleet commanders are equipped with the personnel, materiel, and training required to project credible naval power at sea, ashore, at home, and abroad.

Ceremony imagery, video b-roll, and official remarks are available on the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) at https://www.dvidshub.net/webcast/38076 and the Surface Warriors portal at https://www.surfpac.navy.mil/ .

items.title: IDANG firefighters visits Cambodia to build foundation for future training
items.author: MSgt Mercedee Wilds
items.summary: Idaho Air National Guardsmen, including two fire protection specialists from the 124th Civil Engineer Squadron, traveled to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Sept. 19-26, 2026, to assess fire response capabilities and lay the groundwork for future training through the Idaho National Guard’s State Partnership Program.
items.body:
Idaho Air National Guardsmen, including two fire protection specialists from the 124th Civil Engineer Squadron, traveled to Phnom Penh, Cambodia, Sept. 19-26, 2026, to assess fire response capabilities and lay the groundwork for future training through the Idaho National Guard’s State Partnership Program.

The assessment established a baseline of Cambodian firefighting and rescue operations, equipment, procedures, and incident command systems to identify opportunities for future exchanges between the two organizations.

“The purpose of our fire assessment in Cambodia is to lay the groundwork and establish relationships for potential future training collaboration,” said Tech. Sgt. Thomas Cabalo, a 124th Civil Engineer Squadron fire protection specialist. “We want to better understand their capabilities while identifying opportunities where our organizations can learn from and support one another.”

Throughout the week, the team worked alongside Cambodian firefighters to compare training, equipment, organizational structure and emergency response procedures. Despite differences in geography and climate, Cabalo said the departments respond to many of the same types of incidents and use similar equipment, techniques and command systems.

The exchange also highlighted capabilities Idaho firefighters could learn from, including Cambodia’s use of firefighting and search-and-rescue drones.

“It would be interesting to see how they utilize this equipment operationally and determine whether there are applications that could be beneficial to our own department and potentially influence future equipment decisions,” Cabalo said.

For Cabalo, one of the most significant takeaways was the opportunity to work directly with Cambodian firefighters.

“The thing that stood out to me the most was the pride these firefighters have in their department and in their work,” Cabalo said. “They took the time and effort to bring out their equipment, personnel, and infrastructure to demonstrate their capabilities. You can see that they work hard to accomplish what they do, and they are genuinely proud of what they have built.”

Col. Chhea Pheng, commander of Cambodian Rapid Response Company 711, said the engagement provided an opportunity to exchange knowledge, share firefighting best practices and strengthen cooperation between the two organizations, ultimately improving their ability to serve their communities.

Idaho and Cambodia established their partnership in 2009 through the National Guard Bureau’s State Partnership Program. Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief have remained a focus of the relationship, including bilateral training, leadership exchanges and capacity-building engagements.

Army Capt. Sam Brown, Idaho State Partnership Program director, said face-to-face assessments establish direct connections between officer and NCO counterparts while helping participants overcome language and cultural barriers through shared problem-solving.

“The SPP builds decade-long relationships between Guard and partner-nation members, creating institutional resilience and deep personal trust,” Brown said.

The assessment identified potential areas for future exchanges, including incident management, wildland fire behavior, vehicle extrication, search and rescue, and emergency medical care.

“My hope is that we can establish a solid training plan that leads to multiple training engagements, both in Cambodia and in Idaho,” Cabalo said. “I would like to see this assessment become the foundation for a long-term partnership where our firefighters can continue learning and training alongside one another.”

items.title: Joint Statement from Defence Ministers of the Joint Expeditionary Force: 02 October 2026
items.summary: Defence Ministers of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) and Allies met at Keflavik Air Base, Iceland, today (02 October) to advance the JEF's role as a key pillar of European and Euro-Atlantic security.
items.body:
Defence Ministers of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) and Allies met at Keflavik Air Base, Iceland, today (02 October) to advance the JEF’s role as a key pillar of European and Euro-Atlantic security. Following guidance from Leaders at the Helsinki Summit in March, Ministers agreed upon further action across the JEF’s key priorities.

1. Reinforcing steadfast support to Ukraine through ambitious delivery of the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership.

The JEF Nations remain steadfast in their support for Ukraine. In 2025, the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership was established to deepen cooperation and strengthen collective security. Today, Defence Minister Khamara virtually joined JEF counterparts to mark the successful ongoing delivery of that Partnership. This year, for the first time, Ukraine participated in the JEF’s flagship Lion Protector exercise, with Ukrainian mine countermeasure vessels operating alongside JEF forces to strengthen interoperability, enabling the JEF to benefit from Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience of modern warfare. Defence Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to the Partnership and agreed to deepen Ukraine’s involvement in JEF activities.

2. To further leverage the JEF’s specific geographical focus and collective expertise in operating in the Arctic, High North, North Atlantic and Baltic Sea regions to strengthen NATO’s northern flank

Defence Ministers reaffirmed that the Baltic Sea region, the High North, and the North Atlantic remain the JEF’s core and interconnected area of strategic interest. Joined by Canadian Defence Minister McGuinty, Ministers discussed opportunities to deepen cooperation between the JEF and Canada, noted Canada’s application to join the Framework, and advanced work towards a shared recommendation to JEF Leaders on Canadian membership.

Ministers also agreed the JEF’s overarching policy direction and a common framework for structuring engagement with partners.

3. To further increase the JEF’s deterrence and peacetime activity.

Defence Ministers received an update on the Lion Protector series, conducted across Iceland and Norway this autumn, and welcomed its synchronisation with the UK’s Carrier Strike Group. Ministers reviewed the JEF’s five-year programme of activity and welcomed continued efforts to strengthen coherence with NATO, including work to align JEF response options with NATO regional plans.

Ministers discussed Russia’s hybrid activity against JEF nations and other NATO Allies and agreed to continue developing common approaches through JEF mechanisms. Despite Russia’s unacceptable acts of sabotage against JEF Nations and other Allies, they are resolved to improving our individual and collective preparedness to defend against these threats and will not be deterred from supporting Ukraine. Ministers reiterate that JEF nations do not seek confrontation and pose no threat to Russia, but Russia should be in no doubt that we will defend ourselves.

Ministers also reviewed progress on defence industrial cooperation following two meetings of JEF National Armaments Directors since the Ankara Summit. They welcomed the pace of work to identify practical opportunities for collaboration and the importance of delivering tangible outcomes. Ministers reaffirmed the need for collaboration in reinforcing interoperability, advancing capability innovation, and strengthening shared industrial resilience. Ministers looked forward to receiving concrete proposals ahead of their next meeting. The Single Services continue to deepen military engagement within the JEF, including through work on the Northern Navies concept, in support of the JEF’s five-year exercise plan.

Finally, Ministers reaffirmed the JEF’s vital contribution to a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO. They highlighted the JEF’s unique role below the threshold of Article V, delivering agile and credible responses to emerging challenges while complementing NATO’s deterrence and defence posture. Ministers directed further work to demonstrate the JEF’s contribution to Euro-Atlantic security and ensure the Framework continues to meet the evolving needs of our collective security.

Ministers thanked Iceland for hosting the next JEF Leaders’ Summit in Reykjavik next spring.

items.title: Attention to Detail and Readiness Highlight NMRTC Patuxent River Fall Uniform Inspection
items.author: Maria Scott
items.summary: Active-duty Navy Medicine personnel assigned to Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command (NMRTC) Patuxent River and its subordinate units and detachments across Maryland and Virginia recently completed their seasonal Fall Service Dress Blue uniform inspection, reinforcing military bearing, operational readiness, and the attention to detail carried into daily patient care.
items.body:
Crisp white piping, aligned ribbon racks, and mirror-shined dress shoes marked the arrival of autumn as active-duty personnel from Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command (NMRTC) Patuxent River and its subordinate units and detachments completed their annual Fall uniform inspection.

Active-duty Navy Medicine personnel completed the seasonal evolution locally at their respective duty stations across Maryland and Virginia. Formations took place at command headquarters at NMRTC Patuxent River, Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Unit (NMRTU) Dahlgren, NMRTC Detachment Indian Head, and NMRTC Detachment Joint Base Andrews. These active-duty Sailors serve as the operational military core working alongside civilian and contract staff under Naval Health Clinic (NHC) Patuxent River and its associated branch clinics, representing an integrated total staff of roughly 265 healthcare personnel.

Marking the semi-annual seasonal transition to Service Dress Blues, command leadership thoroughly inspected personnel in ranks. Lt. Thomas Porter, a dental officer assigned to NMRTC Detachment Indian Head, served as the junior officer in charge of the inspection evolution at command headquarters, leading the formation as inspecting officers and senior enlisted leaders evaluated hair and grooming standards, cover placement, gig lines, medals, ribbons, and footwear cleanliness in accordance with U.S. Navy Uniform Regulations. In keeping with longstanding naval tradition, leadership also tested Sailors on their general military knowledge, posing questions on naval heritage and historical milestones to reinforce the foundational legacy of the naval service.

“The professionalism across NMRTC Patuxent River and our branch locations was on full display during this Fall's Dress Blue uniform inspection,” said Capt. Ken Radford, commanding officer of NMRTC Patuxent River. “I was thoroughly impressed with our Sailors across all four sites and the meticulous attention to detail they applied to their uniforms. That exact pride and precision translates directly to the vigilance and meticulous care they provide our warfighters, beneficiaries, and families every single day.”

Beyond tradition and military bearing, the inspection reflects the command’s dual-hatted operational environment and an ongoing commitment to steady self-improvement. Through Navy Medicine, NMRTC Patuxent River maintains the operational readiness of its active-duty personnel to support fleet missions anytime, anywhere. Simultaneously under the Defense Health Agency, those same personnel deliver dependable, patient-centered care across Naval Health Clinic Patuxent River and its outlying clinics to ensure service members remain medically ready to deploy while caring for their families and beneficiaries. By setting a high bar in ranks, the command reinforces the everyday readiness and discipline needed to continually evaluate clinic workflows, elevate the patient experience, and find better ways to serve the military community.

items.title: 94th Army Air and Missile Defense Command hosts PACSIM 26
items.author: SGT Dustin Stark
items.summary: JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii -- Air and missile defense professionals from the U.S., Japanese, and Australian militaries (respectively) gathered at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii, Sept. 21-26, 2026, for the Pacific Simulation for Integrated Air and Missile Defense Modernization simulation event.
items.body:
JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii -- Air and missile defense professionals from the U.S., Japanese, and Australian militaries (respectively) gathered at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii, Sept. 21-26, 2026, for the Pacific Simulation for Integrated Air and Missile Defense Modernization simulation event.

Hosted by the 94th AAMDC at the Missile Defense Agency (MDA) Flight Center, PACSIM provided participants with an opportunity to examine air and missile defense concepts, identify challenges and explore ways to improve integration between the three nations.

The simulation brought together leaders and subject matter experts from across the Indo-Pacific theater to examine how different sensors, command and control systems, and defensive capabilities could contribute to an integrated defense.

Using constructive simulation data provided by the Raytheon Aerospace and Defense Company and the 94th AAMDC, the U.S. and its allies worked through sandbox scenarios to improve understanding of modernized IAMD capabilities and inform future planning.

For the participants, the value of PACSIM extended beyond the simulation itself and helped the participants understand how each nation approaches air and missile defense and how those capabilities could be integrated during future contingencies.

“This year’s PACSIM event invited a trilateral audience to better understand modernized Army IAMD capabilities through the use of a simulation tool,” said Maj. Hazumu Yano, the PACSIM event facilitator assigned to the 94th AAMDC. “As the United States fields new systems, it will be important for our allies in the Pacific to know how we intend to employ these capabilities."

Integrated Air and Missile Defense planners are an integral part of the PACOM mission set. These professionals coordinate defense architecture across multiple domains with the objective of protecting themselves as well as their allies from a wide range of aerial and missile threats.

A major focus of the simulation was to consider how modernized capabilities, combined with integration and data sharing with allies, could change defense designs in the future.

Earlier detection can provide commanders and air defenders additional time to assess a threat and determine which sensor and defensive capability is best suited to respond. The simulation also examined how an integrated network of sensors and effectors could improve the defense of allied critical assets.

“It is the architecture. It’s how we fight,” said Chief Warrant Officer 4 Terry Wood, the 94th AAMDC special plans officer. “It allows us to create a rush network that allows systems to talk between themselves.”

While technology remains an important part of integrated air and missile defense, event coordinators also emphasized the importance of relationships and shared understanding.

Working through potential challenges in a simulated environment allows military professionals to identify differences in procedures, planning and communication before those differences must be addressed during an actual operation.

For leaders and planners, PACSIM provided an opportunity to examine what future multilateral defense designs may look like.

Brig. Gen. William Parker, the 94th AAMDC commanding general, addressed participants during PACSIM and highlighted the importance of continuing to advance air and missile defense capabilities while preparing Soldiers to employ them.

“At the end of the day, we may fight with technology, but people win the fight,” said Parker. “What we choose to do with that technology will determine what that outcome looks like.”

PACSIM 2026 demonstrated the importance of integration and data sharing in forming an effective regional IAMD architecture.

By bringing U.S., Japanese and Australian military professionals together to examine air and missile defense challenges, the event provided participants with an opportunity to strengthen relationships, exchange knowledge and identify ways to improve collective defense.

items.title: Intelligence Leads to Victory at Kings Mountain (7 OCT 1780)
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: On Oct. 7, 1780, a group of American frontiersmen under Col. William Campbell decisively defeated a force of Loyalists under Maj. Patrick Ferguson at Kings Mountain in South Carolina. A triumph of American aggressiveness and fighting skill, their success was also the result of an effective intelligence effort.
items.body:
On Oct. 7, 1780, a group of American frontiersmen under Col. William Campbell decisively defeated a force of Loyalists under Maj. Patrick Ferguson at Kings Mountain in South Carolina. A triumph of American aggressiveness and fighting skill, their success was also the result of an effective intelligence effort.

After the defeat at Camden, South Carolina, in August 1780, American resistance in the region was reduced to localized skirmishing by small partisan bands. These small but fast-moving bands used intelligence and skillful knowledge of local terrain to harass British and Loyalist targets. By September, the major American target was Ferguson and his Loyalist militia. Since May, the British officer had been organizing a force of Loyalists in the western Carolinas. Unwisely, he threatened the Americans, warning that, unless they ceased opposition, he would “lay waste to their country with fire and sword.” This ultimatum only enraged previously neutral or inactive settlers, including the frontier militia known as the Overmountain Men, into joining the American cause.

In late September, around 1,400 of these rugged frontiersmen gathered in what is now eastern Tennessee and moved against Ferguson, who was then located 90 miles to the south at Gilbert Town, North Carolina. As this force, under Colonel Campbell’s field command, marched south, it repeatedly gained and confirmed new intelligence. When the militia reached Gilbert Town, they found no enemy. American scouts scoured the area to make sure the Loyalists were not hiding nearby or setting a trap; instead, they reported that Ferguson had departed a few days earlier. Pressing forward, the scouting parties determined the enemy had moved southeast, crossed the Broad River, and was somewhere between Tate’s Plantation and Kings Mountain.

Over the next week, the Overmountain Men moved south and then east in pursuit of Ferguson’s force. Near Cowpens, about 35 miles west of Kings Mountain, Campbell and his colonels convened to evaluate conflicting reports. Some militia leaders claimed Ferguson was heading toward Ninety-Six, a British stronghold about 90 miles to the south; others thought he was moving toward Charlotte, some 60 miles to the east. On the evening of Oct. 6, Col. James Williams, a South Carolinian militia leader, arrived in camp with additional fresh troops. More important, however, he brought critical intelligence.

As he was raising his militia force, Williams had sent thirty-year-old Joseph Kerr to scout Major Ferguson’s disposition. On Oct. 5, Kerr, who was crippled from infancy, approached the Loyalists’ camp as a harmless beggar, seeking shelter. His lameness allowed him to move freely about the Loyalists without raising suspicion. As they halted for their noon meal, Kerr noted their numbers and learned they were heading for Kings Mountain to encamp. Quietly slipping away, he joined Williams and the rest of the Overmountain Men, providing them with critical intelligence on the enemy’s numbers and intentions.

With Ferguson within their reach, the Americans immediately sent a force of 900 of the best mounted men to fix the Loyalists and continue to develop the enemy situation. As the Americans approached Kings Mountain, a local woman pointed out the spur of the ridge where the Loyalists were camped, which Maj. William Chronicle, from nearby Tryon County, recognized as a former hunting camp. Two captured enemy scouts revealed the location of Ferguson’s picket line. Finally, on the morning of the battle, the Americans captured John Ponder, Ferguson’s fourteen-year-old courier, who was carrying a dispatch to Lord Charles Cornwallis, the overall British commander in the South. The teenager also revealed that Major Ferguson could be identified by a distinctive checked duster.

On the morning of Oct. 7, Campbell’s force attacked Ferguson’s position from all directions. The rugged terrain and persistent rain helped cover the American attack. By the end of the day, Ferguson was dead—Ponder’s descriptor allowed American marksmen to identify and target the British leader—and his force was killed, wounded, or captured. While American tactics and courage overwhelmed the Loyalist force on the battlefield, the constant stream of intelligence had allowed the Patriots to locate a moving enemy, verify every report, identify terrain advantages, and had guided them to the exact place where victory was possible.

Article by Michael E. Bigelow, INSCOM Command Historian. New issues of This Week in MI History are published each week. To report story errors, ask questions, request previous articles, or be added to our distribution list, please contact: TR-ICoE-Command-Historian@army.mil.

items.title: CMSAF announces distinctive beret for Air Force EOD Airmen
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: The announcement took place virtually during the graduation of the inaugural Project MAMBA course at Tyndall Air Force Base’s Silver Flag training site.
items.body:
Published Oct. 2, 2026

Secretary of the Air Force Public Affairs

Chief Master Sergeant of the Air Force David R. Wolfe announced Oct. 2 that Air Force explosive ordnance disposal Airmen will earn a distinctive rust-colored beret, recognizing their specialized combat arms mission and contributions to the joint force. The announcement took place virtually during the graduation of the inaugural Project MAMBA course at Tyndall Air Force Base’s Silver Flag training site. Project MAMBA, short for Multi-domain Airmen for Modern Battlefield Application, is the Air Force EOD community’s redesigned pre-deployment training pipeline. The course incorporates recent combat lessons and prepares EOD Airmen to operate in complex, contested environments alongside joint and coalition forces. “Today’s graduates represent the capability, professionalism and warrior ethos that define our explosive ordnance disposal force,” Wolfe said. “As you prepare to deploy and take on one of the Air Force’s most demanding missions, carry forward the pride and combat identity you have earned. The EOD beret will stand as a visible recognition of that identity and your service to the joint force.”
