items.title: Space Development Agency to Launch 21 More Data Transport Satellites Next Week
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Development Agency is set to launch 21 Tranche 1 data transport satellites on Oct. 5—its fourth Tranche 1 mission since last fall and the first to carry Northrop Grumman-built satellites. The post Space Development Agency to Launch 21 More Data Transport Satellites Next Week appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Space Development Agency is set to launch 21 Tranche 1 data transport satellites on Oct. 5—its fourth Tranche 1 mission since last fall and the first to carry Northrop Grumman-built satellites.

The launch is scheduled for 1:15 a.m. local time from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket. Once in orbit, the 21 spacecraft will join 63 Tranche 1 satellites built by York Space Systems and Lockheed Martin.

The mission represents a few firsts for Northrop. It’s not only the contractor’s inaugural Tranche 1 launch—the company is on the hook for another batch of 21 Tranche 1 Transport satellites and 14 missile tracking spacecraft—but it’s also the firm’s first time delivering and operating such a large quantity of satellites. SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters during an Oct. 1 prelaunch call that based on some of the challenges other providers have had with scaling, he expects there will be some challenges.

“It’s one thing to go through launch and early ops of one, two, maybe even three or four satellites. Twenty-one is a completely different ball of wax,” said Sandhoo, who is also the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for missile warning, tracking, and defense. “We’ll see some issues, but I’m confident the team at Northrop … the issues that pop up, any patches, any updates we have to do, they’re ready to go.”

Since SDA started in 2019 to build out a proliferated constellation of data transport and missile warning satellites in low Earth orbit, the agency has faced setbacks that have delayed launches and fielding timelines. While it had hoped to have all 154 of its Tranche 1 satellites in low-Earth orbit by this summer, supply chain issues and technical challenges on the ground and in orbit disrupted those plans. Sandhoo has attributed many of those slowdowns to the challenges that come with building and launching satellites in large numbers.

“The issue has not been the capability of the system,” Sandhoo told reporters. “The issue has been building them at scale, getting them tested at scale, launching them at scale, doing the launch and early ops at scale. It’s the volume of these things that has been a challenge.”

Following the launch of York and Lockheed’s first spacecraft last year, initial on-orbit checkout and testing took much longer than the four to six months SDA expected. The agency ended up taking a nine-month pause to sort out issues on orbit and make changes on the ground to ensure its next satellites didn’t run into the same hiccups.

In July, SDA resumed Tranche 1 launches, flying York’s last 21 transport satellites. Checkout of those spacecraft went much smoother, Sandhoo said. Since then, the agency has moved control of York’s satellites into its operations center and started doing some limited experimentation. SDA has had some issues transferring Lockheed’s spacecraft to the operations center. To date, it’s only been able to move four, and Sandhoo said the company and SDA are working through the engineering issues to understand the cause and make sure it’s addressed before Lockheed launches more satellites.

“As we get the rest of the architecture, the rest of the planes up, it’s going to get more complicated,” he said. “We need to make sure the understanding is there, the behavior, and the dependability. Being able to get them in the ops and working properly is critical.”

A spokesperson for Lockheed told Air & Space Forces Magazine the company is working closely with SDA to transition the satellites to the agency’s control centers.

“These experiences are an important part of developing new, integrated space systems and we’re focused on ensuring reliability and mission success during this transition, while still moving quickly as a team,” Lockheed said. “We will apply lessons learned from each plane into future efforts.”

While the agency isn’t out of the woods yet in terms of schedule and scaling woes, Sandhoo told reporters he expects that as companies and their suppliers get used to building and flying larger numbers of satellites, their performance will improve. But for now, he said, he’s not satisfied with the time it’s taken to get to this point.

Asked what SDA could have done differently to avoid these setbacks, Sandhoo said it’s possible that for the early tranches of satellites, the agency could have required more insight into the companies’ processes rather than opt for the more hands-off approach it took in its contracting strategy.

“We are trying to get to a place where we can have a capability-driven architecture. We tell them what the system needs to do, and our vendors and our industrial base builds that out to that spec with minimal oversight,” he said. “Maybe we should have, for the first tranche, been probably more intrusive in that process than we were.”

Following the Oct. 5 launch, SDA is eyeing its first Tranche 1 tracking layer mission either in December or early next year. Beyond that flight, it’s hoping to finish the last four launches and have all Tranche 1 satellites in orbit by late spring 2027.

items.title: B-52s Get Prototype System for Beyond-Line-of-Sight Communications
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: Air Force Global Strike Command has fielded a new prototype system for beyond-line-of-sight communications on the B-52H Stratofortress in a step forward for modernizing the Cold War-era heavy bomber. The post B-52s Get Prototype System for Beyond-Line-of-Sight Communications appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Air Force Global Strike Command has fielded a new prototype system for beyond-line-of-sight communications on the B-52H Stratofortress in a step forward for modernizing the Cold War-era heavy bomber.

IRIS, a communications system developed by Outerlink Global Solutions, integrates a satellite communication terminal with other components both on the bomber itself and on the ground, the command said in an Oct. 1 statement. IRIS is meant to make it easier for B-52 crews to carry out their missions and increase their flexibility when carrying out long-range strike missions, Global Strike said.

“The ability to communicate reliably across vast distances is foundational to our global operations,” Maj. Gen. Ty Neuman, commander of the 8th Air Force and the Joint-Global Strike Operations Center, said in a statement. “Fielding IRIS gives our crews a modern tool to stay connected, share information, and execute the mission in dynamic and contested environments.”

The name IRIS is not an acronym, Global Strike said. A 2022 U.S. Strategic Command release on an early demonstration of the IRIS system said it uses Iridium’s high-bandwidth CERTUS broadband service, which is powered by Iridium Next satellites in low-Earth orbit.

The Air Force is now working on a sweeping array of programs to modernize its fleet of 75 B-52s, which are more than six decades old. The bombers still fly with their original 1960s-era Pratt & Whitney-made TF33 engines, which will be replaced with new Rolls-Royce F130 engines under the Commercial Engine Replacement Program. B-52s will also receive a new radar, upgraded avionics, new cockpit displays, and other systems intended to keep it flying at least into the 2050s.

Modern communication capabilities are essential for the B-52 to continue to support global operations and joint force requirements in increasingly contested airspaces, Global Strike said.

“This is about readiness,” Jackie Ford, chief of Global Strike’s rapid capabilities division, said in the statement. “Rapidly fielding capabilities into our operators hands will ensure the B-52 remains ready not just for today’s mission, but for the missions of tomorrow as well.”

The Air Force first showed an earlier version of IRIS could work on a B-52 in June 2022, when the 49th Test and Evaluation Squadron at Barksdale Air Force Base, La., carried out an aerial demonstration on a Stratofortress. Global Strike said a team from the 608th Air Operations Center, also at Barksdale, studied how well voice and data, including images and videos, transferred from the B-52.

After IRIS’s successful demonstration, the command kept working with other Air Force innovation and acquisition units to evolve it from a test case to operational use, including using a Small Business Innovation Research Phase II contract from AFWERX to integrate the system onto the B-52.

The IRIS work transitioned to a formal program in 2023 into a $26 million Strategic Funding Increase contract, which represented Global Strike’s first such deal, the command said.

The command’s rapid capabilities and bomber requirements divisions took the lead on defining what the program’s requirements should be.

The 49th worked with the B-52 System Program Office and Airmen with operational expertise from the 307th Bomb Wing at Barksdale to make sure IRIS developed into a useful system on the bomber. Global Strike said leaders prioritized the program and ensured it moved forward quickly.

By March 2026, IRIS was ready for ground and flight testing which showed it could reliably stay connected while a B-52 was airborne and was technically mature enough to support operational use.

Testing continued, and by the time April began, Global Strike Command had installed multiple IRIS kits on B-52s and delivered them to the 49th to help support training and operational employment.

While IRIS is fielded operationally, Global Strike said, it remains a prototype, and more testing and evaluation will come as the system matures.

“Partnership is what made this possible,” Maj. Gen. Peter Bonetti, director of Global Strike’s strategic plans, programs, and requirements directorate. “We had a clear operational need, the right partner capabilities, and engaged stakeholders working together to deliver capability operators needed and are using today.”

items.title: 7th Air Force Ends ‘Super Squadron’ Test, Returns F-16s to Kunsan
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: After a two-year experiment that created F-16 “Super Squadrons” at Osan Air Base just 50 miles away from North Korea, the U.S. Air Force has returned some of the fighters to its other base on the peninsula. The post 7th Air Force Ends ‘Super Squadron’ Test, Returns F-16s to Kunsan appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
After a two-year experiment that created F-16 “Super Squadrons” at Osan Air Base just 50 miles away from North Korea, the U.S. Air Force has returned some of the fighters to its other base on the peninsula.

The 7th Air Force, which oversees USAF forces in Korea, announced the phased return of F-16s to Kunsan Air Base on Sept. 28. But captions for images released by the 7th state some of the jets returned in May and August.

After the return is complete, there will be two fighter squadrons at Kunsan and one at Osan. Kunsan is about 150 miles from the to the Demilitarized Zone that splits North and South Korea

“The decision to return the F-16s on the Korean Peninsula to a three-squadron structure leverages the strategic advantages of both Osan and Kunsan Air Bases while increasing operational flexibility,” Won Hee Kim, a spokesperson for the 7th Air Force, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.

The Air Force launched its Super Squadron experiment in 2024, shifting F-16s and the associated personnel from the 8th Fighter Wing at Kunsan to the 51st Fighter Wing at Osan. As the experiment began, Osan was divesting its A-10 Warthogs and would have had only a single F-16 squadron left.

The experiment unfolded in two phases, each creating a jumbo squadron of 31 jets instead of the usual 24. It was slated to run through October 2026, but Pacific Air Forces commander Gen. Kevin Schneider announced in April that the test “was successfully completed” and the forces would “reset” to their bases.

Officials did not provide specific reasons for the experiment’s conclusion when they announced it in April.

Super Squadron Background

Under the three-squadron structure, the 7th Air Force has the 36th Fighter Squadron and the 80th Fighter Squadron at Kunsan, and 35th Fighter Squadron at Osan, with an estimated 72 F-16s spread between the two locations—F-16s from Misawa Air Base in Japan began transferring to Osan in a move separate from the Super Squadron experiment.

Those 72 Fighting Falcons represent a sizable chunk of the U.S. Air Force’s 826 or so F-16s: nearly 9 percent.

The fighter wings at Kunsan and Osan both operate F-16Cs and F-16Ds, primarily Block 40 Vipers, an aircraft with modernized features for Suppression of Enemy Air Defense, night operation, and precision strike capabilities.

The Super Squadron aimed to measure maintenance and combat generation efficiencies, commanders said at the time. Lt. Col. Karl Wiest, spokesperson for then-Chief of Staff Gen. David W. Allvin, said in 2025 that the move sought to improve readiness and training while “reducing manpower and logistical support requirements.”

Allvin also sought to reduce excess infrastructure and logistical requirements across the Air Force.

“The Super Squadron test provided valuable data and critical insights for F-16 operations across the U.S. Air Force,” according to an April release.

Neither the 7th Air Force nor the 8th Fighter Wing provided details on the lessons learned from the Super Squadron experiments.

“The Airmen involved in this effort demonstrated a culture of adaptability, innovation, and complemented the Agile Combat Employment model by enhancing flexibility within the force,” Kim wrote.

items.title: Air Force and Space Force Shooting for Historic Recruiting Goals in 2027
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: The Air Force adjusted its fiscal 2026 recruiting goal down by a few hundred enlisted Airmen due to higher-than-expected retention and the number of available training slots—but it is aiming high in fiscal 2027 with its biggest goal for the Active-Duty Air Force in nearly 25 years, and the Space Force is shooting for its biggest goal ever. The post Air Force and Space Force Shooting for Historic Recruiting Goals in 2027 appeared first on Ai
items.body:
The Air Force adjusted its fiscal 2026 recruiting goal down by a few hundred enlisted Airmen due to higher-than-expected retention and the number of available training slots—but it is aiming high in fiscal 2027 with its biggest goal for the Active-Duty Air Force in nearly 25 years, and the Space Force has set its largest recruitment target ever.

In an Oct. 1 release touting its successes in fiscal 2026, the Air Force Recruiting Service said it “met its recruiting goals” and enlisted 31,950 Airmen into the Air Force and 730 Guardians into the Space Force.

That Air Force number is 800 fewer than the 32,750 recruits the service cited in April when it announced it had accomplished its goal five months ahead of schedule. Headquarters Air Force shifted the goal this summer, a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine, as it adjusted to the “realities” of retention and the number of slots available at Basic Military Training. Every military service has an end strength authorized every year by Congress, and if retention is higher than expected, the service can only add so many recruits. BMT also can be limited by resources or available training dates.

The Air Force spokesperson said recruits were not cut but rather added to the Delayed Entry Program where they await their turn to start Basic Military Training. There are currently 15,799 recruits in the DEP, giving the Air Force Recruiting Service a healthy backlog to draw upon to start the new fiscal year.

That could prove crucial as AFRS attempts to pull off a massive 2027. Another spokesperson confirmed its goals for next year are 36,300 non-prior service enlisted Airmen for the Active-Duty force, and 1,402 enlisted Guardians for the Space Force.

The Air Force’s recruiting goal hasn’t exceeded 35,000 since 2003, according to data compiled by Air & Space Forces Magazine. And the Space Force has never aimed for more than 900 new Guardians in its brief history.

Those big totals come as officials across the military say they are seeing historically high interest among potential recruits—and as the Pentagon pursues a major increase in resources and overall end strength.

“In [fiscal 2027], we will grow the force again by an additional 44,000 service members,” Pentagon comptroller Jules “Jay” W. Hurst III said in April. “This growth will provide the manpower needed to employ new capabilities, and it will improve readiness and quality of life by ensuring units are properly staffed for the missions we task them with.”

The Air Force in particular wants to increase its Active-Duty end strength by nearly 9,000, from 321,500 Airmen to 330,400, and the Space Force wants to add 2,800 Guardians, going from 10,400 to 13,200.

In its release, the Air Force Recruiting Service said it will adjust its strategies for 2027 “based on labor market trends, propensity-to-serve data, and career field demand signals.”

In a panel discussion last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Air Force Deputy Chief of Staff for manpower, personnel, and services Lt. Gen. Jefferson O’Donnell said much of the service’s growth would be more “restorative” than “additive,” reversing declines in manning for key career fields.

“We are focused on making sure that we are prioritizing those things like maintenance and logistics and security forces to fill in those spots where we have been taking significant risk across our service,” O’Donnell said.

items.title: Saudis plan assault on Houthis to break Red Sea chokehold
items.author: Timour Azhari and Mubasher Bukhari, Reuters
items.summary: More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized in the offensive, depending on the scale, officials said.
items.body:
Saudi Arabia is planning an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen, with options being considered, including a coastal push to secure the Red Sea shipping route or an assault on multiple fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters.

The operation, expected to be launched in the coming weeks, will be led by Yemeni forces on the ground, which are overseen by Riyadh, and supported by Saudi air strikes, according to six people with knowledge of the preparations.

While the US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh’s operations in Yemen, and some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, the Saudi allies aren’t expected to play a direct role in combat operations, said the people who requested anonymity to discuss security matters.

Saudi Arabia entered neighboring Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the internationally recognized government, which the Houthis had driven out of the capital Sanaa. A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

A key objective of the planned Saudi offensive, which hasn’t been previously reported, is aimed at reversing the rapid gains made by the Houthis last month when they advanced down the coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, according to people with knowledge of the plans who include Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats.

The Saudis are considering two options for the assault, the Gulf and Yemeni officials said: either a narrowly focused attack around Bab el-Mandeb or a broader offensive that also includes synchronized attacks on multiple fronts around Yemen, in the governorates of Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf.

More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized in the offensive, depending on the scale, the officials all said.

Spokespeople for the Saudi and Yemeni governments, the Houthi group and the US military didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment about the Saudi plans.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that’s assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.

Riyadh has concluded it cannot enter new Yemeni peace negotiations with the Houthis while the militants remain in control of Bab el-Mandeb, giving them significant global leverage, the Western diplomats and Gulf official said.

The six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations couldn’t give a precise timing for the launch of the offensive, with their estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November.

Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected an offensive to be narrowly focused and certainly more modest in scope than the Saudi-led operation in 2015 that sought to rout the militants.

“As much [as] they want to vanquish the Houthis completely, they also need to get back to status quo ante before Houthis controlled territory along Bab el-Mandeb,” he added. “Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic.”

The Houthis have become Iran’s most formidable ally in the Middle East since Israel’s degradation of Hezbollah in Lebanon over the past three years.

A Saudi-directed offensive against the group would mark a new flashpoint in a region engulfed by conflict since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel of Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent US-Israeli war on Iran.

Washington, Saudi Arabia’s most powerful ally, is providing military advisers and intelligence, including targeting information, to support Saudi air operations in Yemen, according to one of the Western diplomats.

However, the extent of support may be limited. Reuters has previously reported that US President Donald Trump rebuffed requests by the de facto Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman for direct military support such as air strikes.

Turkey and Pakistan, with whom Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement last month, have provided military equipment that the kingdom is using in Yemen, Pakistani and regional officials said.

Last month, Pakistan sent four cargo planes with equipment including air defense systems, light artillery, drones and anti-drone systems to Aden, the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, a Pakistani government official said.

Pakistani military advisers are also on the ground with Saudi counterparts to support Yemeni forces, according to a second Pakistani official, the Gulf official and a Western diplomat. Turkish drones, bought by Saudi Arabia before the current war, have also been deployed over Yemen, they added.

One of the kingdom’s key concerns in launching a new offensive in Yemen is how to protect its oil facilities and other infrastructure from Houthi drone and missile attacks, according to regional officials who said Riyadh has asked several allies for help with defensive systems.

Pakistan has deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom’s land borders and help with drone and missile interceptions, according to the second Pakistani official, who said the troops arrived in waves beginning last year but also after the recent escalation. Islamabad hasn’t made any decision to send troops into Yemen in a fighting capacity, the official said.

The Pakistani and Turkish defense ministries didn’t respond to requests for comment on their military support for Riyadh.

France, meanwhile, has announced it will send defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.

Any ground operation inside Yemen will rely on the disparate coalition of Yemeni fighting factions that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates armed and trained at earlier stages of the civil war when the conflict ground to a bloody stalemate.

“Many anti-Houthi forces are still not organized or prepared for the kind of sustained offensive required to push back a disciplined Houthi military force. And they are being tested right now, as the Houthis apply pressure across several fronts at once,” said Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha.

Yemeni forces were further fractured last winter when southern fighters backed by the UAE tried to take territory in the east and announce secession plans, leading to their defeat by Saudi-backed fighters after a series of clashes.

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, cautioned that the outcome of any offensive by the Saudis against the Houthis would depend on how ground forces perform.

“The priority so far has been to defend the positions on the ground and stabilize the front, but certainly they will be going on the offensive,” he said. “Success greatly depends on the quality of the performance of the local forces.”

items.title: Lawmakers Push for Bipartisan Solution to Golden Dome’s Funding Crunch
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: Some lawmakers in the Senate are advocating for a more bipartisan approach to paying for the Pentagon’s $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense project, arguing that the effort’s goal of bolstering homeland defenses has support across ideological lines but the process for funding it has been politically charged—leaving the program’s near- and long-term future uncertain. The post Lawmakers Push for Bipartisan Solution to Golden Dome’s Funding Crunch appeared first on <a href="htt
items.body:
Some lawmakers in the Senate are advocating for a more bipartisan approach to paying for the Pentagon’s $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense project, arguing that the effort’s goal of bolstering homeland defenses has support across ideological lines but the process for funding it has been politically charged—leaving the program’s near- and long-term future uncertain.

During a Sept. 29 hearing of the Senate Armed Services Committee’s strategic forces subcommittee, lawmakers bemoaned the Pentagon’s decision to use a controversial funding tool called reconciliation—which allows Congress to appropriate funds with a simple majority vote—to kickstart President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome initiative in 2025. That decision, they argued, took a program whose mission has broad support in Congress and enveloped it in politics.

“Should it have been necessary to go to reconciliation to get this started? I would say no. This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said during the hearing. “I won’t lay fault for why that’s happening, I’m just simply saying we need to get back to a bipartisan approach to this as soon as possible.”

Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said the effort is one of the “most expensive and important initiatives of this government” that has strong support in Congress, making it “very bothersome” that the Pentagon and the White House opted to circumvent the traditional appropriations process to resource it.

And Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) pointed out that while Golden Dome as a program materialized under President Donald Trump’s administration, its roots are bipartisan. The Senate Armed Services Committee inserted language into the Fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act codifying the need for a layered missile defense architecture.

“So, it came from us,” she said.

Yet it was Trump’s announcement in January 2025 that the Pentagon would build an expansive homeland missile defense architecture that brought major attention and funding to idea. First called “Iron Dome For America” and later changed to “Golden Dome,” the vision is for a layered architecture comprised of sensors, ground and space-based interceptors, and interconnected command-and-control systems designed to defeat a range of threats, from drones and more traditional weapons to advanced hypersonic and cruise missiles.

To date, the Pentagon’s strategy for funding the program has been to bypass the annual budget process and rely instead on reconciliation. As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed in July 2025, Golden Dome received $25 billion—90 percent of which it had obligated as of mid-August, according to Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein.

This year, the Pentagon requested $17 billion for the effort as part of a proposed $350 billion reconciliation package, and just $400 million in the normal “base” budget for fiscal 2027. For now, though, there appears to be little political will to pass another spending bill via reconciliation, leaving Golden Dome without a clear path for near-term funding.

That challenge is exacerbated by the fact that the federal government is now operating under a continuing resolution, a stopgap funding measure aimed at avoiding a wholesale shutdown that holds spending at prior year levels. The CR took effect Oct. 1, the first day of the new fiscal year, and because Golden Dome does not have a fiscal 2026 appropriation to serve as its baseline, the program has nothing to fall back on.

Guetlein warned in August that a CR presents a real challenge for the program, and a failure to provide any funding in fiscal ‘27 would be disastrous.

“A CR doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a topline to fall back to to get that percentage of the continuing resolution,” he said during the Space and Missile Defense Symposium, adding that if Congress and the Pentagon can’t find a way to pay for the effort in fiscal ‘27, “there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding.”

During this week’s hearing, Rounds urged his colleagues in Congress to find a solution.

“Let’s get back to a bipartisan [approach], and let’s include it in the underlying appropriations bill,” he said.

Meanwhile, experts testifying in front of the Senate panel agreed that it’s important for Congress to address the funding quagmire, but added that there’s a broader risk that the politicization of the program could make it a target in the future.

Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that even Golden Dome’s name is polarizing and argued that Congress should consider potentially renaming the effort in future policy legislation. He also suggested making steps to institutionalize the project and Guetlein’s acquisition authorities within the broader missile defense enterprise.

In his written statement, Karako noted that Guetlein’s status as a direct reporting portfolio manager, or DRPM—which means he reports directly to Deputy Secretary of Defense Steven Feinberg—is meant to be temporary, and said now may be the time to start thinking about the program’s long-term management and where it should sit within the enterprise after that moniker and its associated authorities fade.

Karako offered that while the Pentagon and Congress could opt to create a permanent entity to oversee Golden Dome, that approach may lead to duplication with other organizations like the Missile Defense Agency and the military services and would take time to establish. But merging Golden Dome with MDA could be a viable solution, he said.

“Whatever the scope of mission for the future air and missile defense of the homeland, its realization and governance will benefit from unity of effort with clear authority, high level access, control of resources, and appropriate acquisition authorities,” Karako said in his statement.

items.title: F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions During Midnight Hammer
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East. Six of the pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities. The post F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions During Midnight Hammer appeared first on <a href="https://www.airandspaceforces.com"
items.body:
Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East.

The pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer, the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities, service officials said.

The Airmen escorted B-2 Spirit stealth bombers that struck the Fordow and Natanz nuclear sites in Iran. The strike package also included F-16 Fighting Falcons and F-35 Lightning II fighters, and pilots from those units received DFCs earlier this year; tanker crews from multiple units have also received the award for supporting the mission. No individual awards have yet been announced for the B-2 aviators who participated in Midnight Hammer.

The DFC recognizes acts of heroism or extraordinary achievement in the air and is the military’s fourth-highest award for heroism.

Six medals were presented on Aug. 31 by the head of Air Combat Command, Gen. Adrian L. Spain, at a ceremony at the Virginia base. The seventh F-22 pilot received their decoration Sept. 22 from U.S. Air Forces in Europe commander Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds for leading the strike package.

The Virginia-based F-22s were among an armada of fighters that escorted the seven B-2s that dropped 14 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator weapons on Iran’s nuclear facilities. Around 125 U.S. aircraft of all types were involved in the mission, which came after a nearly two-week Israeli air campaign against Iran. The stealthy F-22s serve as the Air Force’s premier air-to-air fighters and can use their capabilities to penetrate defended airspace.

“Their job was to provide air superiority,” Spain said, according to an account of his remarks provided by the 1st Fighter Wing. “The bombers and the rest of the support package relied on these Raptor pilots to clear the skies, shield them from surface threats, and ensure a safe route through heavily contested airspace.”

Officials from Air Combat Command, U.S. Air Forces in Europe, and the 1st Fighter Wing declined to provide further details on the mission that earned the pilots their decorations or medal citations, or to publicly disclose pilots’ identities, citing operational security concerns.

“We haven’t awarded many of these in the last few decades, as it’s intended to recognize true heroism and highly exceptional accomplishment in flight, which means that it should be rare, and it is,” said Spain.

Iran’s air force was largely destroyed during the 2026 air campaign against the country, Operation Epic Fury. But even during Midnight Hammer, Iran posed a limited air-to-air threat, with most of its capability consisting of aircraft purchased before the Iranian revolution in 1979. Before the Shah was overthrown and a theocratic government took over, Iran was the largest purchaser of American arms. Iran also has Soviet-designed fighters.

Still, Iran showed the ability to generate some airpower, launching aircraft to attack Gulf countries after Israel and Iran began their air campaign on Feb. 28 of this year, and was able to strike a base in Kuwait used by the U.S. with one of its aging fighter jets.

F-22s from Langley deployed to support Operation Epic Fury and follow-on actions against Iran earlier this year but have since returned.

“It was your support that enabled their excellence—from the maintainers, the operations team, the intel professionals, and the logistics involved,” Spain said. “Let there be no doubt heroism like this is earned by the entire formation. These pilots were the leading edge that day, but the foundation of their success was laid by the hard work of the entire organization in the days prior and every day since. And that’s what Air Force readiness looks like.”

The lead pilot faced “challenging conditions including enemy threats” and “directed the aircraft formation, making critical decisions with limited time and little margin for error,” according to USAFE.

“For more than an hour, [the pilot] remained focused on protecting teammates” and “acted decisively to protect the larger force, and ensured the formation could safely return,” Hinds said. “Their actions helped give the strike package the time and freedom needed to accomplish its mission.”

items.title: Ukraine war fatigue fuels defense-spending downgrade plan in Italy
items.author: Tom Kington
items.summary: Italian military planners risk losing out on billions in funding as government and opposition parties seek to cut defense spending and Ukraine support.
items.body:
ROME — Italian military planners risk losing out on €8 billion ($9 billion) in funding as government and opposition parties seek to cut both defense spending and support for Ukraine.

The plans to limit spending emerged this week as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni continues to be squeezed between NATO spending targets and voter opposition to spending tax payers’ cash on arms not hospitals.

The possible €8 billion shortfall is tied up with Italy’s hot-and-cold approach to a European Union scheme to allow states to exempt a quantity of defense spending from their calculations of annual deficit spending over a number of years.

The so-called National Escape Clause would allow EU states to rearm while not breaking EU deficit rules.

After Meloni’s government promoted the scheme, it then appeared less enthusiastic when the EU finally approved it before Meloni announced this year she would use the extra cash not only for defense but also to cover Italy’s soaring fuel costs.

That was due to generate a defense windfall of between €21 billion and €22 billion thanks to NEC. But the calculation changed on Thursday at a Cabinet meeting when deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini succeeded in pushing the amount down to around €14 billion, a drop of up to €8 billion.

“It’s yet to be made definite but the reduction was agreed,” a government source told Defense News.

Salvini leads the League party which is part of Meloni’s governing coalition and is battling defense spending hikes, opposing sending military support to Ukraine and wants a deal with Moscow to end the conflict in the country.

That contrasts with Meloni’s firm backing for Kyiv and support for Europe’s hardline opposition to Moscow, but she is in a minority in Italian politics. To her right, a new challenger Roberto Vannacci is calling for an end to sanctions on Russia, while among Italy’s left-wing opposition parties, the Five Star party has blamed the Ukraine conflict on a “war mongering Europe.”

A poll of Five Star’s members this month found over 90% opposed European rearmament and believed sending arms to Ukraine was to blame for prolonging the war.

Despite a groundswell of opposition to defense spending in Italy, Meloni has meanwhile committed to NATO’s spending target of 5% of GDP, and she has claimed Italy has reached 2.8% this year, including spending on domestic security.

But details are scant: this year’s budget breakdown has yet to be published.

Meanwhile, Rome said in August it would request €8 billion euros in cheap loans from the European Union’s SAFE defense funding program, down from its original intention to ask for €14.9 billion euros in loans.

In a parliamentary hearing on Sept. 23, the CEO of Italian defense giant Leonardo said he was a big fan of SAFE loans, since they guaranteed cash for defense programs with few complications.

“I believe SAFE is the first, real useful measure that Europe has come up with,” said Lorenzo Mariani.

“The money has never been much and it’s been complicated. Now SAFE is moving a lot of money and using a system which we believe is not complex like other European schemes have been,” he added.

“Portugal is buying FREMM frigates built by Leonardo and Fincantieri thanks to SAFE funds,” he said.

Mariani said he had talked up the virtues of SAFE loans to the Meloni government.

“SAFE is very positive. The use of it does not depend on me. I have made proposals which I hope are accepted by the government,” he said.

One analyst said Rome needed to make up its mind about spending.

“The government needs to take important decisions about NEC and SAFE loans which were granted to all member states after years of requests by Italian governments,” said Alessandro Marrone, who heads the Defence Security and Space Programme at Rome think tank IAI.

“The government should have implemented its decision by now to enable better planning by the Italian defense ministry. It’s urgent. This is not just about NATO targets but about filling gaps left in Europe next year by U.S. pull-outs and now following through on Italy’s desire to send naval vessels to defend the Red Sea.”

Tom Kington is the Italy correspondent for Defense News.

items.title: Taiwan’s first two F-16V fighter jets arrive to bolster defenses against China
items.author: Ann Wang, Reuters
items.summary: The first two of a batch of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets ordered in 2019 arrived in Taiwan on Friday after months of delays.
items.body:
TAITUNG, Taiwan — The first two of a batch of 66 new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets ordered in 2019 arrived in Taiwan on Friday after months of delays, helping to strengthen an air force that has to scramble almost daily to shadow China’s military.

Taiwan faces a rising military threat from Beijing, which claims the democratically governed island as its own territory. Taipei has complained of repeated delays to weapons ordered from the United States, its most important international backer and arms supplier.

The delivery, to Taitung’s Chihhang Air Base on the mountainous east coast, comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei, despite Washington saying there has been no change in policy.

The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at noon (0400 GMT).

“This is an important development in strengthening Taiwan’s air defense capabilities,” President Lai Ching-te wrote on Facebook, thanking the United States for its support.

Speaking to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Defence Minister Wellington Koo said there would be other new F-16Vs arriving soon, though he did not give details.

In 2019 the U.S. approved an $8 billion sale of Lockheed Martin F-16V fighter jets to Taiwan, which would take its F-16 fleet to more than 200. But issues such as software problems delayed delivery of the planes.

The arrival of the first two aircraft came almost exactly a week after US President Donald Trump met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

Trump said in May, after meeting Xi in Beijing, that he was holding a new $14 billion package for Taiwan in abeyance, though he did approve one worth $11 billion in December 2025.

China threat level

U.S. officials believe a Chinese invasion of Taiwan before 2028 is increasingly unlikely, people familiar with U.S. thinking told Reuters. Taiwan holds its next presidential election in early 2028.

“China’s intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed,” Koo said.

Taiwan also has an ambitious domestic weapons program, including building what is eventually planned to be eight submarines, drawing on expertise and technology from several countries, including the United States and Britain.

The first boat, the Narwhal, had been due to be delivered to the navy in 2024, but the program — Taiwan’s first attempt to build a submarine — has been hit with delays.

Chen Jeng-horng, chairman of CSBC, which is building the vessels, told reporters in southern Taiwan’s Kaohsiung that the Narwhal was undergoing its final tests before delivery.

“Of course, the sooner the better for all parties,” he added, without giving a timeframe for when the navy would get it.

Advanced new fighter

The new F-16V jets have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters, though Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan its most advanced fighters such as the F-22 or F-35.

The United States is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations.

Beijing has repeatedly told Washington to stop arming Taiwan. The Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment on the arrival of the F-16s.

“We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan,” a U.S. State Department spokesperson said when asked about the new F-16s.

items.title: French Air Force plans loyal wingman flight in 2028 in sovereign AI push
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: The French Air Force plans to fly crewed fighter jets in collaboration with AI-powered combat drones in 2028, under project Hypairion.
items.body:
PARIS — France’s Air Force, together with the country’s Directorate General for Armament and the agency for defense artificial intelligence, plans to fly crewed fighter jets in collaboration with combat drones in 2028, part of a project to experiment with AI in combat aviation dubbed Hypairion.

The project seeks to develop open, modular architecture for combat aircraft and sovereign AI technology that gives the government greater control over the tech, rather than having to rely on companies for critical systems, said Col. Cédric, head of the Air Force capability-development office, in a press briefing here on Thursday.

As AI becomes more powerful, the likes of Airbus and BAE Systems in Europe and General Atomics and Anduril in the United States are leveraging the technology to develop collaborative combat aircraft, also referred to as “loyal wingmen.” While many of those projects are company-driven, the French project would keep some of the critical technology under state control.

“What Hypairion is really about is equipping the Air Force and our platforms with architectures that are open, modular and owned by the government,” Col. Cédric said. He was identified only by his first name, in line with the Armed Forces Ministry’s policy for military staff. “Our goal is to move away from proprietary systems that lock down sensors and weaponry.”

The Ministerial Agency for Defence AI will be in charge of providing sovereign AI technology for the project in several areas, particularly command and control as well as mission autonomy, said Col. Thibault, deputy director for AI applications at the agency, known as Amiad. He described mission autonomy as AI that assists pilots with mission planning, in-flight decisions and post-mission analysis.

Amiad already uses AI to coordinate different platforms in the French Army’s Pendragon robotics project, and proposes to create an industrial hub for Hypairion where both traditional aerospace firms and smaller startups can interact with the project, an approach tested in Pendragon.

“The point of the Hypairion project is for the French state to retain control of the overall architecture and to be able to integrate the most capable startups or industrial companies,” Col. Thibault said. He said companies might join and leave the project, while Hypairion retains its capabilities in-house.

The Air Force is modifying two Mirage 2000s fighters at Mont-de-Marsan airbase to become AI test beds, adding a new computer that will allow to test “all kinds of use cases” starting by the end of the year, according to Col. Cédric. Mont-de-Marsan in southwest France is home to the Escadron de chasse et d’expérimentation, a dedicated fighter squadron for testing and evaluation.

Development will be incremental, and the first stage of Hypairion won’t necessarily be about having an operational capability, but will look at areas such as energy consumption and system interfacing, Col. Cédric said. First use cases being considered include using AI to optimize flight paths or tactical decisions such as when to deploy air-to-air or air-to-ground weapons.

The unmanned aircraft set to fly in 2028 will be a test platform and may not be the future wing-man drone planned for France’s Rafale jet as part of the fighter’s future F5 standard, though the experimentation will help pick a suitable platform later in the decade, Col. Cédric said.

The DGA has set a target data of 2033 for the first version of the Rafale F5, but will work on collaborative platforms within the framework of the current F4 standard before then, said General Engineer of Armaments Sébastien, in charge of the Rafale program at the directorate.

The goal of integrating AI on the Rafale is to help crews manage the “absolutely phenomenal cognitive load” to maintain future operational superiority, he said. The armaments engineer cited the Talios laser-designation pod from Thales, set to be delivered to the armed forces in 2027, as a concrete application of AI, able to scan an area and provide a fighter crew a list of potential targets.

Col. Cédric described a hypothetical future in which a fighter crew would carry out a mission in the morning, in between missions identify an adaptation against an enemy countermeasure, and take off again in the afternoon with updated software. That will require system architectures to evolve, he said.

The French Air Force officer likened future manned and unmanned platforms to “flying computers” on which the keyboard, screen or software could be changed without compromising security. The goal of the architecture being developed within Hypairion is to separate the flight-safety aspect from the ability to carry out missions, he said.

The Air Force doesn’t envisage a future with only unmanned aircraft, for both ethical and operational reasons, according to the colonel, who said the decision to deploy weapons remains a human one, and AI can make mistakes. “Humans can be augmented or supplemented by AI, but the assessment of the operational situation, tactical judgment, and so on, these are still entirely the domain of humans.”

As the Air Force prepares the Rafale F5 standard, “a true mid-life overhaul of the aircraft,” focus areas include adequacy of hardware resources, as the system needs to be able to handle complex calculations, Sébastien at the DGA said. Another focus is system openness, meaning “the armed forces must be able to tailor artificial intelligence according to their own needs and so dispose of an open system.”

The Rafale’s F4 standard already includes an initial level of openness through a tablet connected to the mission system, and the F5 standard will seek to broaden the scope of data available to the tablet, give it access to the mission system’s computing resources, and improve the ability to interface with onboard communication systems and data links, according to the DGA engineer.

“This in particular will make it possible, and without waiting for the deployment of the F5 standard, to control autonomous combat platforms from the Rafale,” Sébastien said.

While France relies on Dassault Aviation and other major industrial partners for the Rafale to develop AI in the fighter’s major systems, the armed forces want to ensure operational autonomy, meaning having “the ability to tailor the AI to the specific operational needs of the theater,” the engineer said.

Hypairion will work on a road map covering usage concepts, doctrine, scaling up the work force as well as the actual equipment, resulting in a first full-scale trial of collaborative combat drones flying alongside fighter jets in 2028, according to Col. Cédric.

“The challenge for the Air and Space Force is ultimately to determine what a fighter squadron will look like in 2035 or 2040, once all these systems are potentially integrated into the squadron,” Col. Cédric said. “Today, it’s actually quite rare to come across computer scientists in a fighter squadron. Perhaps tomorrow, that will be a daily occurrence.”

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

items.title: From Strategic Logic to Practical Implementation: A Phased Agenda for U.S.-ROK Shipbuilding Cooperation
items.summary: U.S.-ROK cooperation on shipbuilding should be structured so that it strengthens U.S. maritime industrial capacity, makes commercial sense for Korean shipbuilders, and survives the political and regulatory constraints on both sides.
items.body:
The United States faces growing pressure to rebuild maritime industrial capacity. Naval shipbuilding programs continue to struggle with long production timelines, workforce shortages, supplier fragility, acquisition instability, and legal barriers. Maintenance backlogs remain significant. Geopolitical competition is also placing greater emphasis on sealift, sustainment, and the ability to generate maritime capacity at scale in a prolonged contingency. These pressures have renewed interest in how U.S. allies and partners might contribute to the maritime industrial base.

South Korea is one of the world's leading shipbuilding nations, with large-scale commercial production, as well as extensive experience in ship design, yard management, modular construction, supplier integration, and increasingly digitalized manufacturing. As a result, U.S.-ROK cooperation in shipbuilding and maritime innovation has become a more prominent subject of policy discussion.

RAND's recent conference on U.S.-ROK Cooperation on Shipbuilding and Maritime Innovation reinforces that the central issue is not whether cooperation makes strategic sense. What matters more is how to structure cooperation so that it strengthens U.S. maritime industrial capacity, makes commercial sense for Korean shipbuilders, and survives the political and regulatory constraints on both sides. The harder question: What forms of cooperation are compatible with U.S. defense and industrial priorities and commercially viable for Korean shipbuilders? Balancing short-term needs against long-term industrial priorities is also a challenge.

The United States is simultaneously pursuing multiple objectives in allied shipbuilding cooperation that do not clearly align. One objective is to increase maritime capacity in the near term. This includes addressing production bottlenecks and maintenance backlogs. A second objective is to rebuild domestic industrial resilience over the long term by strengthening shipyards, supplier networks, labor pipelines, and production know-how inside the United States. A third objective is to preserve sovereign control over critical defense capabilities, technologies, and wartime production. All this must occur within political, legal, and budgetary constraints shaped by Congress, labor interests, and local industrial constituencies.

These objectives might reinforce each other in some cases, but they also come into tension. Measures that provide near-term capacity may not always build long-term domestic resilience. Efforts that maximize domestic control may not produce capacity quickly. And policies designed to protect U.S. industry may, in some cases, limit the use of allied capabilities that could offer additional capacity in the short run. This tension was a central theme of the RAND conference. Discussions focused on trade-offs: What kinds of cooperation would help solve immediate problems? Which forms would support the domestic industrial base over time? And where do political or regulatory barriers limit the available options?

Measures that provide near-term capacity may not always build long-term domestic resilience.

The Core Problem Is Broader Than Yard Capacity. It's Performance

The most immediate constraints are not only physical infrastructure but the underlying industrial system: workforce shortages, especially in the skilled trade and mid-level supervisory ranks; weak or fragile ecosystems; production inefficiencies; and acquisition practices that often generate design instability and schedule delays. In many naval programs, construction begins before designs are sufficiently mature, producing cascading effects on cost and productivity.

In Korean shipbuilding, firms generally stabilize design early and bear greater responsibility for integration and execution. The U.S. Navy strives to incorporate the latest technology and combat systems in each of its ship classes. With extended design timelines and pressure to begin construction, design changes are often continuously adopted well into production. Government oversight is extensive, typically not in ways that improve productivity. This is a significant mismatch. Without changes in U.S. program structure or design discipline, Korean firms' comparative advantages may be undermined.

Some discussion at the RAND conference cited examples such as the Littoral Combat Ship, the Expeditionary Fast Transport, and the Constellation-class frigate as reminders that foreign design lineage or allied participation does not guarantee successful outcomes. In several cases, adapted designs were heavily modified in the U.S. system to accommodate Navy-driven requirements. This increases risks and reduces the benefits of using an established baseline.

This has two implications for cooperation with allies. First, external industrial capacity alone will not solve U.S. shipbuilding problems if domestic bottlenecks in design, management, workforce, and supply chains remain unaddressed. Second, the most useful contributions from allies may not be limited to ship output itself. Process discipline, production methods, workforce development models, supplier integration, and digital tools may matter as much as physical construction in strengthening U.S. performance over time.

From a U.S. policy perspective, that distinction is important. If cooperation is framed primarily as overseas substitution for domestic capacity, it is likely to face political resistance and may do little to strengthen the U.S. industrial base in the long run. If instead cooperation is structured to improve domestic production capability, it may not produce the near-term output that is needed.

The Near-Term Need Is Real, but So Is the Political Constraint

The United States wants to increase maritime capacity more quickly, but it also wants to rebuild that capacity domestically. These goals are not always in sync.

Some argue that if the objective is to “pulse” additional ships into the fleet in the near term, then allied or foreign yards may be the only practical option for certain platforms. Others argue that Congress is less likely to accept large-scale offshore construction of combat-relevant ships, even if it would accelerate delivery. The short-term desire to get more ships quickly and the long-term commitment to domestic shipbuilding seem to be misaligned in significant ways.

That political constraint was reflected in repeated references to the proposed Golden Amendment in the FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act, which would restrict foreign construction of U.S. military vessels and major hull or superstructure components. Whether or not the provision is enacted in its current form, it captures a broader congressional concern: U.S. shipbuilding is not only an industrial issue but a sovereign capability one as well. This concern is especially addressed in segments of the fleet tied to combat power and strategic deterrence. This suggests that allied cooperation models will need to fit within a political framework that strongly favors domestic industrial rebuilding.

A broader congressional concern is that U.S. shipbuilding is not only an industrial issue but a sovereign capability one as well.

Demand Signal, Risk, and the View from Industry

From the Korean industry perspective, demand predictability emerged as a central issue. Meaningful industrial participation in the United States would require substantial commitments: facilities, supply chains, trained personnel, management systems, and in some cases technology protection arrangements. Korean firms are not likely to make such investments based only on strategic rhetoric. They will look for evidence that demand is stable, policy direction is durable, and the business case is credible.

One lesson learned from the RAND conference was that Korean firms already have order books extending several years into the future and are not under pressure to enter lower-margin, higher-risk business lines unless conditions justify doing so. Uncertainty is not limited to overall demand. It includes the volatility of U.S. surface ship acquisition plans, unclear program requirements, the risk of political transitions, and the challenge of building supplier ecosystems in a high-cost environment.

It is also important to note that the issue is not only U.S. demand: Korean shipbuilders themselves face long-term questions about future market conditions and labor constraints, creating incentives to globalize and diversify. That suggests some areas where U.S. and ROK interests may align—but not at any price. If the United States wants allied firms to invest in ways that support domestic industrial revitalization, it will need to improve the quality of its demand and address barriers to industrial participation.

A More Practical Starting Point: Auxiliaries, MRO, and Industrial Enablers

Large-scale foreign construction of battle force ships remains politically difficult and, in many cases, operationally sensitive. A key takeaway from the RAND conference was the identification of a limited set of areas where U.S. need is high, barriers are lower, and cooperation might also support domestic rebuilding.

Auxiliary ships and strategic sealift vessels are frequently cited as plausible candidates. These platforms are urgently needed and less politically sensitive than frontline combatants. They could serve as pilot programs, allowing the United States and its allies to test cooperation models without forcing immediate resolution of the most sensitive sovereignty and technology issues.

Maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) also emerged as a serious area for cooperation. U.S. sustainment backlogs are significant, and legal restrictions on foreign MRO support are less stringent for auxiliary vessels than combatants. There exist examples where MRO efforts on auxiliary ships have been completed in foreign yards, and this additional capacity could greatly help U.S. backlogs. It is important to emphasize industrial enablers rather than end items when the United States considers allied cooperation in shipbuilding. For example, workforce exchanges, supervisory training, supplier development, additive manufacturing, digital design tools, condition-based maintenance, and digital twins may be less visible than ship construction, but they may align more directly with the long-term goal of improving U.S. industrial performance.

It is important to emphasize industrial enablers rather than end items when the United States considers allied cooperation in shipbuilding.

Policy Priorities for a U.S.-Aligned Cooperation Agenda

If U.S.-ROK shipbuilding cooperation is to support U.S. government and Navy priorities, several principles should guide policy.

Start with Clearly Defined U.S. Objectives

Policymakers should distinguish among near-term fleet support, long-term industrial revitalization, sovereign production needs, and alliance management. Cooperation that addresses one objective may not address another.

Focus First on Lower Friction, Higher-Value Areas

Auxiliaries, strategic sealift, MRO, supplier partnerships, workforce development, and selected component or block production appear more consistent with both operational need and political feasibility than large-scale offshore construction of battle force ships.

Use Cooperation to Improve Domestic Performance, Not Only Add External Capacity

The most useful allied contribution may be in transferring production methods, training models, supplier integration, and digital processes that help strengthen U.S. shipbuilding over time.

Improve Demand Predictability

If the United States wants sustained allied industrial participation, it will need more credible procurement signals, greater consistency in shipbuilding plans, and better alignment across Congress, the Navy, and the executive branch.

Address Enabling Conditions

Visa rules for skilled personnel, legal clarity for technology protection, and practical support for supplier localization and labor engagement will matter if industrial cooperation is expected to move beyond concept.

Keep Political Sustainability in View

Cooperation that is perceived as bypassing U.S. labor or weakening domestic yards is unlikely to endure. Cooperation that helps build domestic jobs, industrial capability, and production resilience is more likely to attract support.

items.title: US leaders send mixed messages to Indo-Pacific nations
items.author: Gordon Arthur
items.summary: U.S. military allies in the Indo-Pacific region are wary of President Donald Trump's apparent overtures to China's leader Xi Jinping.
items.body:
CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — Army officials from 25 different Indo-Pacific nations recently met in New Zealand to hammer out cooperative defense strategies. Simultaneously, the top political leaders in the United States were sending conflicting messages about its partnerships in the region.

The 50th Indo-Pacific Armies Management Seminar (IPAMS) was held in Auckland in late September, and it emphasized “practical cooperation, interoperability and regional partnerships.”

This year’s IPAMS theme was that “the sum is greater than the parts: security and deterrence in the Indo-Pacific.”

“Across this region, land forces are the backbone of deterrence, security cooperation and the connective tissue that binds nations together,” said Lt. Gen. Joel Vowell, deputy commander of U.S. Army Pacific.

“When our armies train, communicate and plan collectively, we generate a deterrence effect that is far stronger than any individual nation could achieve alone,” he added.

Brig. Hamish Gibbons, New Zealand’s deputy Chief of Army, struck a similar chord, saying collective strength comes from trusted relationships, and a shared commitment to the security of the Indo-Pacific region.

That region covers more than half the Earth’s surface and comprises 40 nations, including China.

At exactly the same time as IPAMS was being held, President Donald Trump was welcoming Chinese Chairman Xi Jinping onto American turf.

Afterwards, David Perdue, the U.S. Ambassador to China, relayed one head-scratching moment when he revealed Trump had offered to sell military weapons to Beijing. Officials in Washington have since said there are no actual plans in the works to that end.

Ryan Hass of the U.S.-based Brookings Institution said the offer amounted to a break with longstanding Washington policy.

“If there was any ambiguity about whether President Trump views China as a security threat, this disclosure by Perdue puts the question to rest,” Hass wrote on X, formerly Twitter. “Trump’s offer to sell weapons to China will be unsettling to American partners at the pointy edge of China’s spear.”

Unease was already fermenting as Trump withholds large arms sales packages to Taiwan.

In an open letter published on Sep. 22, Rupert Hammond-Chambers, President of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council, warned of the damage being caused by Trump’s arms freeze on Taiwan.

“The Trump administration has let the fox in the henhouse,” Hammond-Chambers wrote. “Telegraphing sensitivity to the Chinese position on Taiwan this past spring, Trump has empowered China to affect his decisions.”

He said the notion that appeasing China will result in a quid pro quo concession is false, since the Chinese Communist Party outright rejects any responsibility to change its own aggressive behavior.

Some analysts chalked up the cozy Trump-Xi interactions as an expression of the U.S. president’s penchant for pomp.

“Trump may say things off the cuff that make Taipei (and U.S. allies) uncomfortable, but that will not change the long-term trajectory and trend of U.S. security commitments to Taiwan,” Drew Thompson of the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore wrote.

The arms-sales comments, he said, would not affect cross-strait relations, as they are not progressing towards Beijing’s primary objective of peaceful unification.

Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

items.title: Guidance: Veterans of the LGBT Ban: Financial Recognition Scheme
items.summary: Guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme for veterans who served under, and were impacted by, the Ban on LGBT personnel in HM Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.
items.body:
LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme

Data detailing scheme progress which will be shared on a monthly basis.

Data as of 28/09/26:

Total individual applicants*: 1,780

*Applicants may have more than one case due to there being two payment types.

Total decisions made on cases: 2,309

Value of total payments made: £59,305,000

The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme was recommended by the LGBT Veterans Independent Review which was published in July 2023.

The LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme is a payment scheme open to those who served under and were directly impacted by the Ban on LGBT personnel serving in the Armed Forces from 1967 to 2000.

This page provides information and guidance on the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme, including eligibility and how to apply.

Types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments

There are two types of Financial Recognition Scheme payments:

1. LGBT Dismissed or Discharged Payment. This payment is for those who were dismissed or administratively discharged because of the Ban, including officers who were ordered or instructed to resign or retire by their respective Service Board. 2. LGBT Impact Payment. A payment to recognise other experiences of those who served under the Ban, as outlined in the Financial Recognition Payment Types and Tariff Table. (LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme Rules, Annex B).

Applicants are strongly encouraged to read the scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above before starting an application.

How to Apply

The Ministry of Defence encourages all eligible applicants to submit their applications online.

An app for the scheme can be accessed on Defence Gateway from 13 December 2024.

This platform will ensure that your data and any uploaded documents are secure. The app dashboard will keep you updated about the status of your application.

The online application process has two steps:

Step 1 : Register for a Defence Gateway Account so you can access the online Financial Recognition Scheme application form.

Step 2 : Sign in to your Defence Gateway account and submit your Financial Recognition Scheme application form via the Financial Recognition Scheme app.

Hard copy applications

If you would prefer to submit a hard copy (paper) application form, read scheme rules and guidance on how to apply for a financial recognition payment above.

Hard copy application forms can also be obtained from Veterans UK .

Freephone (UK only): 0808 1914 2 18 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)

Telephone (overseas): +44 1253 866 043 (8am to 4pm, Monday to Friday)

Help with applying to the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme

Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion have partnered with the LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme to provide support to veterans who are applying to the scheme.

These charities can assist with completing the application form, provide guidance on writing the necessary evidence and answer any questions applicants may have.

Royal British Legion

Phone: 0808 802 8080

For more information on the support the Royal British Legion can offer, visit Royal British Legion - Applying for restorative measures for LGBTQIA+ Veterans .

Fighting with Pride

For more information on the support Fighting with Pride can offer, visit Fighting with Pride LGBT Financial Recognition Scheme .

Veterans Welfare Service

Additional support is also available from the Veterans Welfare Service (VWS) who provide information, guidance and support to veterans and their families, as well as supporting veterans through a network of case managers across the UK and Republic of Ireland.

To find out more, visit Veterans Welfare Service or contact the Veterans’ Helpline using the details below.

Other restorative measures

For information on non-financial restorative measures visit LGBT veterans: support and next steps .
