items.title: Six Scottish soldiers buried in France 108 years after their deaths
items.summary: MOD War Detectives used DNA evidence to identify two of the fallen, four remain unknown though one was identified as having served with the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders whilst the other three likely served with the Gordon Highlanders.
items.body:
Relatives gathered in France today to witness the burial with full military honours of two Scottish soldiers of World War 1 and four of their unknown comrades.

Private ( Pte ) George Fleming Brock and Pte Percy Todd, both 11th Battalion, Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders, were laid to rest alongside four unknown soldiers 108 years after they were killed in action during the German Spring Offensive in 1918.

Pte Brock of Dunipace, West Falkirk, was serving an architectural apprenticeship with the Stirling firm of Messrs Bruce & Livingston when he enlisted in June 1916. Only a month after joining the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders in France, he was seriously wounded by gunshot and spent several months recuperating in hospital.

He rejoined the battalion in January 1918. Two months later the Germans launched a huge offensive on the Western Front. On 28 March 1918, Pte Brock’s battalion were holding positions in the area of Tilloy-les-Mofflaines, when they were overwhelmed by intense bombardment. It was on this day that Private Brock lost his life, aged just 19.

Pte Todd of Radford, Nottinghamshire, was a draper’s manager at Bryan’s Drapery in Isleworth, London, when he enlisted in November 1915. He was living with his wife, Alice, who he had met eight years earlier at work. Pte Todd was also seriously wounded shortly after joining the battalion, on the first day of the Battle of Arras in 1917. After a long recovery, he rejoined his battalion in February 1918, but lost his life less than two months later during the German Spring Offensive, on 5 April 1918.

In 2023, during an archaeological survey on a site in Tilloy-les-Mofflaines the six men were recovered. Found with them were a variety of artefacts, including regimental insignia from the Argyll & Sutherland Highlanders, and from the Gordon Highlanders. After extensive historical research and DNA testing, two of these casualties were identified as Private Brock and Private Todd. The two men were buried alongside four others who could not be identified.

The service was organised by the MOD ’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre ( JCCC ), also known as the ‘ MOD War Detectives’ who work to identify the recovered remains of British military casualties.

Nicola Nash, MOD War Detective said:

Private Brock and Private Todd have both been buried today 108 years after they were killed. With half a million British servicemen still missing from World War 1, every identity we make is a huge achievement. It has been a real privilege to give closure to their families and lay these heroes to rest with honour.

David Royle, Recoveries and Ceremonies Manager at CWGC , said:

For 108 years, these six men lay where they fell on the battlefield. It is a privilege and a source of great pride for the CWGC to have recovered them and worked alongside the JCCC in the effort to restore their identities. While four of these soldiers sadly remain unidentified, they are not forgotten. We will care for their graves, and for those of Private Todd and Private Brock, in perpetuity, ensuring that future generations have opportunity to honour and remember their sacrifice.

items.title: Graves of five soldiers killed in Normandy identified
items.summary: Five missing soldiers of World War 2 who were killed during the Battle of Normandy now have named graves after Rededication ceremonies were held on 29 and 30 September 26, and 1 October 26.
items.body:
The graves of five soldiers who went missing during the Battle of Normandy have been identified and were rededicated this week. A commemorative service honouring all five men, was also held at the British Normandy Memorial in Ver-sur-Mer (30 September 26).

Rededication services took place at CWGC St Charles-de-Percy War Cemetery for Private ( Pte ) George Chapman of 1st Battalion The Herefordshire Regiment (29 September 26), at CWGC Bayeux War Cemetery for Private Vincent Coia of 7th Battalion The Seaforth Highlanders and Lance Corporal ( LCpl ) Reginald Cyril Dewey of 4th Battalion The Lincolnshire Regiment (30 September 26), at CWGC Hottot-les-Bagues War Cemetery for Serjeant ( Sjt ) Frederick Albert Harrison of 1st Battalion The Dorsetshire Regiment and at CWGC Ranville War Cemetery for Corporal ( Cpl ) Henry Thomas Read of 8th Battalion The Rifle Brigade (1 October 26).

Members of the Chapman, Dewey and Read families were present at their relatives’ rededication service. The Coia and Harrison families were not able to attend, but a poignant message from Reg Harrison, the 95 year old younger brother of Sjt Harrison, was read out at his graveside in Hottot-les-Bagues War Cemetery.

Although I didn’t know my brother very well, as I was only young when he left home to join the army, I’m very proud of him and what he achieved, and what he went onto do for his King and country. It was soldiers like Fred that helped us win the war, and keep us safe. Always in my thoughts. Your young brother, Reg.

The services were organised by the Ministry of Defence’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre ( JCCC ), known as the ‘War Detectives’, and were supported by serving soldiers from 5th Battalion The Rifles, 2nd Battalion The Royal Anglian Regiment and 2nd Battalion The Royal Regiment of Scotland.

Rosie Barron, JCCC Caseworker, said:

It has been an honour to have organised these rededication services and to have played a part in giving these families answers as to what happened to their relatives. The local community in Normandy has been very welcoming of both the families and the military party. For them the Battle of Normandy is not just commemorated but celebrated as the moment that they regained their liberty after four long years of occupation. The sacrifices made by these men were not in vain. There are many graves in Normandy which may yet be identifiable with further investigation, so this work will continue into the future.

Reverend Paul Collins CF, Chaplain to 5th Battalion The Rifles, conducted the services.

Reverend Paul Collins said:

It is my privilege to be able part of these rededication services. These brave soldiers gave their lives in the events following D-Day which led to the liberation of France and the defeat of the Nazis. It is fitting that due to the hard work of the JCCC Commemorations Team and others, we now know who these soldiers were and where they are buried. The graves now bear their names for all those who visit in the future to see and remember.

All five men had previously been commemorated on the Bayeux Memorial to the missing. The CWGC has now replaced their headstones with named markers and will care for them in perpetuity.

Dr James Wallis, Head of Commemorations at the CWGC , said:

The Commission’s staff consider it a privilege to care for the now-identified graves of these five soldiers who were killed in the aftermath of D-Day during the Battle of Normandy. The impact of loss upon the respective families of these casualties still resonates strongly – so we are thankful to those who instigated each identification and furthermore to the work of partner organisations which has led to this outcome and brought us together today.

items.title: 30% boost to UK military transport aircraft availability under new deal
items.summary: MoD extends £190 million contract with Airbus to maintain the RAF's A400M Atlas fleet, boosting aircraft availability while sustaining over 350 UK jobs.
items.body:
£190 million contract extension with Airbus to support RAF’s A400 Atlas fleet, retaining more than 350 UK jobs.

Agreement set to increase the number of mission-capable A400M aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.

Britain’s air defence will be boosted under new deal.

A 30% improvement in availability for the RAF’s tactical and strategic airlift fleet will be delivered under a £190 million contract extension between the Ministry of Defence and Airbus.

The extension will see Airbus continue its maintenance, repair and support services for the RAF’s A400M Atlas fleet from its UK Support Centre at RAF Brize Norton.

As well as sustaining more than 350 UK jobs, the extended contract is set to deliver a significant boost to operational capability and will increase the number of fully mission-capable aircraft available each day from 10 to 13 by the end of 2027.

Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:

This contract extension is a vote of confidence in British engineering, and the workforce at Brize Norton and Carterton who keep our A400M fleet flying. By boosting availability of these aircraft, we’re strengthening the RAF’s ability to conduct global operations and deliver on NATO commitments when it matters most, while backing UK jobs and delivering value for money for taxpayers.

This contract extension is a vote of confidence in British engineering, and the workforce at Brize Norton and Carterton who keep our A400M fleet flying.

By boosting availability of these aircraft, we’re strengthening the RAF’s ability to conduct global operations and deliver on NATO commitments when it matters most, while backing UK jobs and delivering value for money for taxpayers.

The A400M Atlas is a cornerstone of the UK’s air mobility capability, supporting operations ranging from humanitarian relief to rapid troop deployment.

Continued support at RAF Brize Norton ensures the fleet remains ready to meet these demands without interruption, forming part of the government’s wider commitment to strengthening the UK’s defence industrial base and value for money in defence contracts.

Air Cdre Si Young, Head Air Mobility in National Armaments Materiel, said:

This contract will deliver continued improvements in A400M fleet availability, building on the growth that we have delivered over recent years and giving our Armed Forces the capability they need while offering excellent value for money to taxpayers, supporting a platform that is at the heart of the RAF’s operations now and into the future. It reflects the strength of our partnership with Airbus and our shared commitment to supporting the continued growth and success of the A400M fleet, both now and in the years ahead.

This contract will deliver continued improvements in A400M fleet availability, building on the growth that we have delivered over recent years and giving our Armed Forces the capability they need while offering excellent value for money to taxpayers, supporting a platform that is at the heart of the RAF’s operations now and into the future.

It reflects the strength of our partnership with Airbus and our shared commitment to supporting the continued growth and success of the A400M fleet, both now and in the years ahead.

The 31-month extension to the Medium-Term Contract means support services will continue until April 2029, sustaining more than 240 Airbus staff and 110 primary sub-contract staff.

Kata Escott, Managing Director of Airbus Defence and Space UK, said:

Airbus is proud to be a trusted partner to the Ministry of Defence, and this contract extension reinforces that commitment. The A400M Atlas is the backbone of Air Mobility. Our highly skilled teams work side by side with Royal Air Force personnel and are fully focused on enhancing operational readiness, keeping the fleet mission-ready.

The contract builds on the work of the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to UK defence over the next four years. The plan will drive sustained investment across British industry ensuring the UK’s defence sector remains a cornerstone of the country’s economic renewal.

items.title: Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment in the Coast Guard
items.author: Sarah Weilant
items.summary: The authors evaluate the Coast Guard’s sexual assault and sexual harassment prevention and response strategies, victim support services to support recovery efforts, and accountability mechanisms.
items.body:
Holistic Study and Analysis

ResearchPublished Oct 2, 2026

This research was conducted within HSOAC, a federally funded research and development center operated by RAND under contract with DHS.

Sexual assault and sexual harassment (SASH) threaten the safety, trust, and cohesion essential to mission readiness in the U.S. Coast Guard. The authors evaluate the Coast Guard’s SASH prevention and response strategies, victim support services to support recovery efforts, and accountability mechanisms.

Sexual assault and sexual harassment (SASH) threaten the safety, trust, and cohesion essential to mission readiness in the U.S. Coast Guard. Investigations, internal reviews, and high-profile reports have highlighted systemic challenges in how the service prevents, responds to, and accounts for these behaviors.

In response, Congress directed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to commission an independent review of the Coast Guard’s approach to SASH. The authors conducted this study to provide an impartial, evidence-informed assessment of the service’s policies, programs, and institutional practices related to SASH. Separately, the Coast Guard conducted its own Accountability and Transparency Review, commissioned by the Commandant in July 2023, which produced 33 recommended actions to address harmful behaviors and strengthen accountability across the service. The authors examine Coast Guard efforts in light of those findings and recommendations while also identifying areas of progress, persistent gaps, and opportunities for structural improvement.

The purpose of the overall project is to evaluate the Coast Guard’s prevention and response strategies, victim support services to support recovery efforts, and accountability mechanisms for SASH. The authors assess the Coast Guard’s policies, how responsibilities are distributed across programs, and how requirements are executed in practice across a geographically dispersed workforce. Particular attention is given to transparency, command involvement, and the extent to which current systems prevent sexual assault and harassment and support both survivor needs and institutional accountability.

- The Coast Guard’s SASH efforts are constrained less by an absence of programs than by how those programs are structured, integrated, and resourced.

- The most foundational concerns involve fragmented policy architecture and data. SASH-related policy is distributed across three distinct directives, with no single integrating framework.

- Data on SASH incidents are similarly fragmented across multiple tracking systems with differing definitions and reporting standards, which limits the Coast Guard’s ability to assess trends, evaluate what is working, and identify where risk is concentrated.

- Prevention and leadership present related challenges. The Coast Guard’s prevention activity is largely training-centric, with success measured by course completion rates rather than demonstrated changes in behavior or risk.

- The response and support system faces ongoing challenges. Survivors and stakeholders expressed continued concern about long investigative timelines, limited visibility into case status, and inconsistent communication.

- Quantitatively, official sexual assault reporting rates have been relatively stable in recent years, but survey-based estimates of prevalence consistently exceed official report counts, indicating that underreporting remains a significant concern.

- Fragmented policy architecture limits coherence, clarity of authority, and accountability. One option would be to establish a single authoritative instruction consolidating SASH prevention, response, recovery, and accountability; another would retain the existing program-specific instructions while introducing a formal governance body to coordinate them and track implementation.

- Prevention is treated primarily as training compliance rather than as a sustained capability. One option would reframe prevention as an enterprise capability with measurable outcome targets; another would require individual programs to articulate how their activities reduce risk.

- Variable training quality, consistency, and focus limit prevention effectiveness. One option would establish a tiered model based on unit risk; another would build risk-based triggers into existing policy.

- Commanders are expected to foster safe and accountable unit climates, but policy provides limited behavioral specificity and no structured accountability mechanisms. One option is to articulate specific behavioral expectations for leaders in policy and to reinforce those expectations through professional development and evaluation.

- Response systems have improved, but trust remains fragile due to communication, transparency, and timeline challenges. One option is to standardize communication practices across the response system; another would focus on reducing investigative timelines through process improvements.

- Resource constraints create a reactive system with limited capacity for prevention and sustained engagement. One option would assign new billets or assignments based on risk and geographic access; another would expand capacity through augmentation strategies.

- Data fragmentation and governance challenges limit evaluation, oversight, and organizational learning. One option would move toward an integrated data environment; another would clarify data stewardship and improve interoperability across existing systems.

items.title: AI Data Center Siting on Federal Lands
items.author: Jennifer Buckley
items.summary: The U.S. government is opening federal land for data center development. In this report, the authors explore how the government could facilitate the siting and construction of data centers on federal land within the context of energy constraints.
items.body:
A new RAND data center siting rubric helps federal agencies screen and rank potential sites based on energy feasibility.

The U.S. government, spurred by a 2025 executive order, is moving quickly to open federal land for artificial intelligence (AI) data center development and directing agencies to identify suitable sites. But energy availability—not just available acreage—is a binding constraint that will determine which sites can realistically support large-scale AI infrastructure.

RAND researchers evaluated 12 U.S. Department of War sites offered for data center leases, compared them with 17 U.S. Department of Energy sites, and developed a cost model to estimate energy infrastructure expenses across 31 candidate locations. A stakeholder workshop stress-tested these findings and informed public-private partnership guidance.

Most sites will require major energy investment.

- Across both departments, nearly every candidate site lacks sufficient existing generation capacity to power a gigawatt-scale data center without significant new infrastructure.

Site rankings shift depending on scale and financing.

- No single site dominates under all conditions. Sites in the southwest perform best for most scenarios, while several northeastern sites consistently rank at the bottom.

Energy costs rival facility construction costs.

- At the gigawatt scale, energy infrastructure expenses are comparable in magnitude to data center construction costs, making energy planning a primary—not secondary—driver of site selection.

Unresolved conflicts can become national security risks.

- A workshop exercise found that community opposition, litigation, and infrastructure disputes at a federally approved data center site could escalate into overlapping legal, political, and security crises that threaten development.

When screening potential sites for development:

- Use a site-screening framework that ranks candidates on energy costs, grid interconnection feasibility, and infrastructure readiness before solicitations are issued.

- Request that bidders describe how they will meet the Ratepayer Protection Pledge—the commitment that data center energy costs will not raise electricity rates for consumers.

- Treat energy infrastructure as a parallel, coequal workstream alongside civil construction in all requests for lease proposals rather than as a subordinate component to be resolved after a lease has been awarded.

When enabling public-private partnerships:

- Develop formal policy guidelines for data center public-private partnerships covering site-specific engagement, risk allocation, security responsibilities, and decommissioning obligations.

RAND researchers applied a previously developed energy suitability framework covering energy supply, energy systems, supporting inputs, environmental conditions, and governance factors to 12 U.S. Department of War sites. They then developed a quantitative energy cost model to estimate the present-value cost of powering a 1-gigawatt data center across 31 candidate sites using four generation scenarios. Sensitivity analyses tested how rankings change under varying assumptions about compute scale, the cost of capital, and cooling requirements. A structured stakeholder workshop with 14 federal and industry participants, including a scenario-based Day After exercise, generated inputs for public-private partnership guidance.

items.title: UK leads major Joint Expeditionary Force Exercise as defence ministers meet in Iceland
items.summary: The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.
items.body:
Hundreds of British personnel train with allies from the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to counter rising Russian threat in Exercise Lion Protector 26.

Training takes place across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea, with Royal Marines conducting the first exercise in the Faroe Islands since the Second World War.

Comes as the Defence Secretary meets JEF counterparts in Iceland, with Canada and Ukraine also in attendance.

The UK is ramping up its defence of the High North and Baltic to combat Russian hybrid threats with the Joint Expeditionary Force conducting major exercises across the region.

Allies from the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which is led by the UK, have conducted Exercise Lion Protector 26, which saw forces train across the North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic Sea to protect critical national infrastructure, strengthen joint command and control, and counter emerging threats.

From the data cables that connect the UK to the world, to the energy infrastructure that powers homes and businesses, the North Atlantic and High North are vital to our national security.

It comes as the Defence Secretary today meets with his JEF counterparts at a summit in Keflavik, Iceland, where ministers will progress discussions on Canada’s application for membership of the JEF Framework.

Ministers will also discuss deepening cooperation on countering hybrid threats, furthering industrial collaboration, and support to Ukraine through the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership. As Canada and Ukraine continue to cooperate closely with JEF, Canadian and Ukrainian ministers will also be in attendance.

Part of Exercise Lion Protector 26 saw Royal Marines from the UK’s Special Operations Maritime Task Group conduct the first exercise since the Second World War on the Faroe Islands, alongside Danish forces.

Marines and their Danish allies carried out maritime interdictions, amphibious landings, and vertical ascent training on the Faroes, which was the location of a key Royal Marines deployment during the Second World War.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:

The North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the Joint Expeditionary Force is so vital to our defence. From conducting amphibious landings on the Faroe Islands, to deploying a standing headquarters north of the Arctic Circle, our recent JEF exercises have shown how Britain is working with our allies to enhance NATO’s defence of the region in the face of rising Russian threats. I was also delighted that we welcomed our Canadian and Ukrainian counterparts to the summit as JEF seeks to expand its cooperation with these crucial allies.

The North Atlantic, High North, and Baltic are the frontline of the UK’s security, which is why British leadership of the Joint Expeditionary Force is so vital to our defence.

From conducting amphibious landings on the Faroe Islands, to deploying a standing headquarters north of the Arctic Circle, our recent JEF exercises have shown how Britain is working with our allies to enhance NATO’s defence of the region in the face of rising Russian threats.

I was also delighted that we welcomed our Canadian and Ukrainian counterparts to the summit as JEF seeks to expand its cooperation with these crucial allies.

Lion Protector launched in August with a rehearsal of a multi-national maritime escort operation stretching the length of the Baltic Sea. Warships and aircraft from Denmark, Latvia, Sweden and the UK escorted a Danish vessel carrying military equipment to Latvia, testing the JEF’s ability to coordinate rapidly across sea, land, air, cyber and space.

The UK’s Standing Joint Force Headquarters coordinated activity across the High North and Baltic Sea region, deploying north of the Arctic Circle in Norway to test its ability to command allied forces at speed and range.

JEF is a UK-led coalition of ten like-minded nations comprising high readiness forces configured to respond rapidly to crises in support of NATO security. JEF brings together the UK, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden to secure the Baltic Sea, North Atlantic, Arctic and High North for NATO.

Today’s summit builds on the JEF Leaders’ Summit in Helsinki in March where leaders agreed to reinforce steadfast support to Ukraine through ambitious delivery of the JEF-Ukraine Enhanced Partnership.

It also builds on the Prime Minister’s discussions with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Støre this week about the hybrid threat Russia poses.

Exercise Lion Protector 26 comes ahead of the Atlantic Future Forum and the International Sea Power Conference, both taking place in Oslo in November.

items.title: Air Force Adjusting Plan for Maintenance Career Overhaul from Just 7 AFSCs to 14
items.author: Matthew Cox
items.summary: The Air Force will officially kick off a major overhaul of maintenance career field next year with a pilot program, but the plan for the revamp is still evolving—while officials once intended to condense 50 aircraft maintenance specialties down to just seven, now they are targeting 14 Air Force Specialty Codes, according to Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell. The post Air Force Adjusting Plan for Maintenance Career Overhaul from Just 7 AFSCs to 14 appeared first on <a href="https://www.a
items.body:
The Air Force will officially kick off a major overhaul of maintenance career field next year with a pilot program, but the plan for the revamp is still evolving—while officials once intended to condense more than 50 aircraft maintenance specialties down to just seven, now they are targeting 14 Air Force Specialty Codes, according to Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell.

Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that the sweeping effort will be “a multiyear transformation” how the Air Force recruits, trains, and develops its maintenance force, suggesting it will be quite a while before that transformation is complete.

“The 2A career field strategy is on track to initiate [an 18-month] pilot test in mid- to late-2027,” said Bell, who added, “It’s going to be a yearslong effort for this to take place.”

The service first revealed its career field transformation plan for maintenance Airmen in January 2025. The strategy called for enlisted Airmen to start out on a generalist track—a single Air Force Specialty Code—where they will focus on applying the most common maintenance skills such as recovering and fueling across multiple airframes. Once Airmen reach the rank of Senior Airman and are preparing to become noncommissioned officers, they would become a specialist in one of six non-aircraft-specific areas:

- Avionics and Electrical, which combines avionics with the electrical side of the Environmental and Electrical (E&E) specialty

- Aerospace Ground Equipment, which will look the same as it does now

- Advanced Mechanical, which combines crew chiefs, fuels, hydraulics, and the flight line side of engine maintenance

- Crew Support Systems, which combines ejection seat systems with the environmental side of E&E

- Fabrication, which combines aircraft structural maintenance, aircraft metals technology, and nondestructive inspection.

- Intermediate-level engines, for maintainers dedicated to intermediate-level engine maintenance.

The New Plan

In the revised plan, the initial phase is similar. It will train maintainers entering the Air Force as aviation maintenance technicians, or AMTs, for their first 18 months of service, focusing on maintenance fundamentals for multiple airframes. The initial phase will also emphasize that the skills they are learning will ground them in the importance of aircraft sortie generation, which is a key focus of the service’s strategy to generate and sustain airpower even if under attack, Bell said.

“We’re an Air Force. We fly, fix, fight, and win. And the first thing that we want to be able to do is make sure that as all of our maintainers come in, they understand what sortie generation is about,” Bell said. “If you can’t get the aircraft off the ground, then what are we really here for?”

Maintenance Airmen will then transition into a specialty track where they will select from one of 14 different specialties, Bell said. The Air Force would not release the new specialty list because it is still refining how it will be organized, according to an Air Force spokesperson. There will be six specialties that are “aircraft-agnostic,” but it’s unclear how they will be different from the original six, the spokesperson said. Another eight specialties will be split among three different aircraft groups:

- Tactical Lift/Rotary

Air Force officials refined the plan to offer more specialties after meeting with maintenance Airmen as part of the effort’s feedback-gathering campaign that began in January.

“We stood up 10 different working groups; we brought in almost 280 different maintainers from across the Air Force to help us refine the strategy and the specifics,” Bell said. “It was long list of things that we went through.”

The revised plan offers maintenance Airmen the option to change their specialty, which is currently based on their score on the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery test that the majority of enlisted Airmen take while still in high school, Bell said.

“How well they did on that ASVAB test could probably determine what career field they went into and where they were going to spend the next 20 years of their life; something just doesn’t sit right about that,” Bell said. “And if we have the ability to now say, hey, ‘this may be where you scored and what you were selected for, but maybe now with a little more maturity, and now that we have shown you some other things, maybe there’s a different path still within the aircraft maintenance career field … maybe you want to choose this specialty over another.’ So, I’m really excited about that aspect of it. There is a little more optionality that also matches up with Air Force needs.”

Eventually, maintainers in the specialty track will have the opportunity to apply for the master aviation technician, or MAT, track—a more specialized pipeline designed to create a smaller force of highly skilled maintainers who will focus on fixing more complex problems on specific aircraft, Bell said.

But the highly selective pipeline is only designed for a “small percentage of maintenance force; that’s going to cultivate them into cross-functional technical experts on a specific aircraft.”

“That small percentage of folks will help us ensure that as people move around, that MAT group of folks will be that core group of folks that we lean on to be those very technical experts to solve some of the hard breaks, the hard problems that might go on the aircraft,” Bell said.

When it was first revealed, the new strategy sparked concerns among current and former Air Force maintainers that the new design could dilute expertise across the career field and reduce local leaders’ ability to solve complex maintenance problems.

“I’m not going to say that that is not a valid concern, but with any change, you’re going to have some amount of pushback to it,” Bell said, adding that that is why the service sought feedback from current maintainers.

“I take all input, and that’s the reason why we have asked the major commands to send me your brightest people who can represent you, who are going to be constructive disruptors,” Bell said.

“To the maintenance Airmen that said, ‘I’m a naysayer and I don’t believe you in this’: give me your input and then help us try to mitigate that,” Bell added. “We can’t continue to do what we’re doing now and think that we’re going to get a different result.”

Critics also question how the Air Force would switch to the new model amid a shortage in maintenance manning.

Bell said that a key benefit of the 2A career field transformation is it will instill in young maintainers the importance of aircraft sortie generation similar to the way Air Force is stressing “airmindedness” in Basic Military Training and tech school to ensure Airmen understand they have a role in generating combat airpower.

“This particular line of effort that we’re doing right now with the two-way career field strategy speaks to retention because we believe that as more maintainers come in and then we train them up in this way, this ability to be sortie generators up front is going to add to their motivation and their reason for being,” Bell said.

“People want to add value, and their ability to be sortie generators early will show that they can add value—that’s why this two-way career field strategy, I believe, is going to be a benefit for us in the retention area.”

items.title: US Navy awards RTX’s Raytheon $24.4B for SM-6 missiles amid stockpile concerns
items.author: Mike Stone, Reuters
items.summary: The deal for the SM-6 interceptors comes as the Pentagon pushes to replenish munitions stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East.
items.body:
RTX’s Raytheon unit won a multiyear contract worth up to $24.4 billion to produce Standard Missile-6 interceptors for the U.S. Navy, the service said on Thursday, as the Pentagon pushes to replenish munitions stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East.

The five-year contract, which includes two additional option years, the Navy said, is meant to provide a steady and reliable supply of the SM-6, a missile that can carry out both offensive strikes and missile defense missions.

The SM-6 award is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued this year to pressure contractors into ramping up output. It follows a $20.7 billion provisional multiyear deal for Raytheon’s AMRAAM air-to-air missiles in late September and a $58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July.

The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster while surging production. They are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritize weapons production over shareholder returns.

Industry executives have warned that Congress has not yet appropriated funding for the deals, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.

RTX has said it has invested heavily to keep up with rising demand. It has expanded its skilled workforce, strengthened partnerships across the defense industrial base and automated production, with the aim of significantly increasing output for near- and long-term needs.

Raytheon says the SM-6 is the only combat-proven weapon that can perform anti-air warfare, anti-surface warfare and ballistic missile defense. It has been fired from a range of Navy ships as well as from land-based launchers.
