items.body:
Dartmoor firing times

Information on Dartmoor Training Area's firing times.

Ministry of Defence and Defence Infrastructure Organisation

4 July 2013

30 September 2026 — See all updates

Dartmoor six week firing times: 28 September to 8 November 2026

Do not touch any military debris it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) or police.

Warning signals: red flags by day and red lamps by night, indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries, which are marked by red and white poles. When warning signals are displayed do not cross the range boundary.

Learn more about accessing MOD training areas safely.

Dartmoor guaranteed public access

The Defence Training Estate: DTE South West (including Salisbury Plain)

items.body:
The White Book for foreign service advisors and defence attachés

Commonwealth Defence Liaison Staffs and Foreign Service Attachés accredited to London.

Ministry of Defence and Cyber & Specialist Operations Command

1 June 2012

30 September 2026 — See all updates

The White Book (September 2026)

Commonwealth Defence Liaison Staff and Foreign Service Attachés accredited to London

This publication is no longer publicly available and is only provided on this site for access by authorised personnel and legitimate defence agencies.

Previous users are now referred to the ‘London diplomatic list’ on the Foreign & Commonwealth Office website at: Foreign embassies in the UK . The list contains all embassies and high commissions with the addresses, all the senior staff, telephone and fax numbers, plus email and website addresses.

‘The white book’ is available on the MOD UK Intranet for users who have obtained the necessary permissions to access the Internet version.

Defence Section London Level 6, Zone J Main Building Whitehall London SW1A 2HB

items.title: Defenders of the Force: How 121st SFS defenders build strength through struggle
items.author: A1C Samir Harris
items.summary: U.S. Air Force Capt. Jeffrey Lazar, 121st Security Forces Squadron commander, Master Sgt. Sean White, 121st SFS defender, and Airman 1st Class Easton Frost, 121st SFS defender, share their experiences serving as defenders at Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center, Michigan, June 17, 2026. Security forces defenders maintain 24/7 readiness to safeguard force assets, personnel, and combat airpower projection.
items.body:
ALPENA COMBAT READINESS TRAINING CENTER, Mich. — When a Security Forces defender straps on a ballistic vest in the quiet early morning, a slight shift takes place. It isn’t just equipment fastened over standard-issue gear; it’s a commitment to being the barrier between possible threats and the force. For the Airmen of the 121st Security Forces Squadron (SFS), putting on that vest means assuming a role defined by heavy rucks, tough conditions, and an unrelenting duty to protect.

"The mindset you have to step into is to be able to understand that you are the first and last line of defense for protecting the force, to allow combat air power to get into the air," said U.S. Air Force Capt. Jeffrey Lazar, commander of the 121st SFS. "Security forces is a very demanding career field. You're asking young 18-year-old kids to put their lives on the line and make life-or-death decisions at a moment's notice."

Lazar, who served 20 years enlisted before commissioning, understands the job's weight extends far beyond the tactical vest. The drive to push through long hours, extreme heat, and physical exhaustion comes from a devotion to what’s behind the perimeter line.

"As a defender, a lot of times it's not what's in front of us that bothers us; it's the people and the things that we're protecting behind us that keep us going," Lazar said. "It's remembering what's back home that we're protecting—those freedoms and liberties that we are here to preserve."

That drive comes from a shared grit built through brutal field conditions and endless hours on shift. When the rain starts pouring, legs get heavier and heavier, and the gear digs in, all that's left is the plain willpower to keep moving and get the job done.

"High stress in the field is the greatest teacher," said U.S. Air Force Master Sgt. Sean White, a defender with the 121st SFS. "You don't fully understand it until you're doing it in the field, feeling the weather, and feeling the emotions of each other. Those grueling days peel back layers of each person until you're raw, to the fact that you understand each other from a brutal concept."

White, who has served through multiple deployments and field exercises alongside the same Airmen throughout his career, found the unit's real strength in its culture of mutual accountability and personal investment.

"This career field is 100% what you get out of it," White said. "When I put my vest on in the morning, the mindset that I step into is honoring those who have come before me. I look to my left and to my right, and seeing those who wear the same vest motivates me more than anything else."

That shared purpose beats across all ranks, from senior leadership down to the newest Airmen walking onto the flight line. As junior Airmen learn the ropes, they quickly grow under constant pressure and forge a bond with their team that they can’t replicate anywhere else.

"When I put my vest on every morning, I flip the switch—I become a defender," said U.S. Air Force Airman 1st Class Easton Frost, a defender with the 121st SFS. "It means I have to do everything required to make sure the mission gets done. The brotherhood that you get in security forces is really like no other; we become one unit."

Whether balancing tactical decision-making at the command level or managing ground defense in demanding operational conditions, the defenders of the 121st SFS remain bound by a shared identity—one symbolized by the beret they earn and the force they safeguard.

"You aren't a defender until you've earned that badge and earned that beret," Lazar said. "The beret is what signifies and separates us from everybody else. A lot of people—everybody that wears that beret—earned it, and that signifies that we are the defenders of the force."

items.title: UAE turns to Russian shadow airline for missions in Africa: Investigation
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: The company behind these planes, Aviacon Zitotrans, has been sanctioned by the United States, Canada and Ukraine for its support in Russia’s war effort.
items.body:
VIENNA — The United Arab Emirates, a Western darling for security cooperation in the region, appears to have regularly used Aviacon Zitotrans, a sanctioned Russian airline linked to the Kremlin’s military and paramilitary operations, over the course of the past year, a Defense News investigation shows.

Analysis of thousands of flight records as well as gigabytes of leaked internal company documents, aviation filings and emails suggest a link between the sanctioned aircraft and more than 100 missions flown on behalf of the UAE government and its royal family since mid-2025.

The Russian company behind these planes, Aviacon Zitotrans, has been sanctioned by the United States, Canada and Ukraine for its support in Russia’s war effort. Previous reporting also revealed its role in sustaining Moscow’s mercenaries in Africa. The specific planes that pop up in the flight logs of UAE’s operations have been separately designated as blocked property by the U.S. government.

This article is the second in a multi-part series that uncovers the peculiar network of front companies, airlines and Soviet-era freight planes.

The UAE’s apparent use of a military-linked Russian cargo airline, alongside its role as a hub for Russian sanctions circumvention, runs contrary to Western efforts to isolate Moscow internationally and cut the Kremlin off from cash flows it needs to maintain its war against Ukraine.

Flight tracks collected by Defense News show that Aviacon Zitotrans’s Soviet-era Ilyushin Il-76 aircraft flew missions linking the UAE to destinations in Africa, following the same routes and operational patterns as those used by other operators that have been tied to the UAE’s support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war. Several flights operated out of UAE military bases rather than civilian airports, implying a government connection.

Defense News reached out to the UAE embassies in Vienna and Washington, to the Abu Dhabi Media Office and the UAE’s foreign ministry for comment on the Aviacon Zitotrans links, but received no response. The airline itself also did not respond to a request for comment.

Other flights flown by Aviacon Zitotrans aircraft and identified by Defense News appear to have flown from the UAE to a private airstrip in eastern Pakistan known as Chandana Airstrip or Al Habieb Airport, which previous reporting has tied to the royal Al Nahyan ruling house of Abu Dhabi. The airstrip does not appear in online ICAO/IATA code databases or Pakistan’s Civil Aviation Authority lists. International reporting has identified it as a gateway to the Gulf royal family’s falconry hunting grounds in Pakistan.

Sparse videos and images exist on the internet of the airfield. Defense News reviewed footage showing large portraits of Gulf monarchs and Pakistani politicians next to the apron and framed in a plush airport waiting room, along with plenty of UAE flags flying alongside Pakistani ones. UAE personnel are flown in ahead of the royals’ use of the airstrip, according to a private plane tracker’s 2022 investigation.

When not operating on behalf of the UAE, Aviacon Zitotrans flies missions for the Russian government, including the shipment of weapons around the world. Leaked internal documents viewed by Defense News show that the airline has delivered combat helicopters to Southeast Asia, armored personnel vehicles to Turkey, and received a special exemption from the Russian government to fly missiles and their warheads.

The company lists “government and military airlifts” as one of its areas of operations on its website, touting that the Il-76 planes it uses are “capable of operating from short and unpaved runways” and “achieved an excellent reputation for its versatility and operational reliability.”

The cabin and rear ramp “provides smooth loading/unloading for many kinds of rolling stock, such as armored personnel carriers (APCs), utility trucks, trailers etc,” the company’s website explains.

“Aviacon Zitotrans specializes in using Il-76 aircraft, which are very helpful, very sturdy aircraft for transporting cargo and transporting people,” said Margaux Garcia, senior analyst with C4ADS, a U.S.-based nonprofit organization specializing in analyzing illicit networks. “They were originally built to be military transport aircraft, so it makes sense that they’re being used for that purpose.”

The company’s Russia-linked operations in Africa have previously attracted attention and prompted the U.S. government to sanction the airline. Sub-Saharan Africa was the main theatre of operations for the infamous Wagner Group, which has been rebranded as Africa Corps following the death of its leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin.

While most Western countries have cut trade with Russia and its state-affiliated entities to a minimum, and the European Union has banned all Russian aircraft from its airspace, the UAE government maintains friendly commercial and diplomatic relations. As a consequence, the country has turned into a hub for Russian sanctions circumvention and foreign procurement, a trend confirmed by the leaked Aviacon Zitotrans air waybills Defense News examined, which routinely showed the procurement of Western goods, including sanctioned electronics, through the Gulf monarchy.

Previous reporting by Reuters has also identified Dubai’s gold markets as a crucial lifeline for Russia, given its exclusion from global payment systems such as SWIFT.

At least three Aviacon Zitotrans-affiliated aircraft have flown routes that match known patterns of UAE government-sponsored missions since September 2025: RA-76842, RA-76502, RA-76846. Another aircraft, RA-76834, flew a mission connecting the UAE’s Sweihan Air Base to Bosaso, Somalia, a known Emirati logistics hub used for weapons shipments into Africa before Somali authorities canceled the relevant agreements with the UAE in January 2026.

“It perfectly makes sense within their business model that they would work for any kind of group that would be willing to fund them. It’s a similar type of work to the work that they seem to do for Russia. So it makes sense that they would expand into this other market,” said Garcia.

All three aircraft flying the vast majority of apparent UAE-chartered missions are explicitly listed by the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control as directly blocked property. Any other Aviacon Zitotrans airframes, including all that may have touched UAE territory on their Russian missions, are blocked by extension due to their connection to the company.

Most flights generally followed the same pattern: The aircraft would first depart a UAE airfield, usually the joint civil-military airport at Al Ain, Abu Dhabi airport, or, more rarely, a military base in the UAE. It would then fly south and west to the Gulf of Aden, where its transponder track would disappear. It would then reappear at the same location over the Gulf of Aden, flying back to the UAE later that day or a few days later.

“If you notice that all of these planes that are run by the same airline all drop off of coverage, then that’s a notable pattern — especially if it happens that most other airplanes are able to travel through that area without dropping coverage,” said Garcia, whom Defense News showed its findings and data. “So it’s not a signal issue. It’s not a coverage issue. That suggests perhaps they are intentionally turning off their transponders; they’re hiding their activity.”

In total, Defense News identified well over 100 Aviacon Zitotrans sorties that had telltale characteristics of UAE government-linked cargo operations.

Defense News used a commercial aircraft tracking archive including ADS-B transponder and MLAT location data to follow the aircraft in question, building an extensive database of almost 9,000 flights conducted by a number of shadow airlines globally since early 2025. Each flight was manually reviewed. The data is often spotty due to deliberate obfuscation techniques or limited coverage, requiring pattern-matching and secondary sourcing through local reporting, ground photography and satellite imagery.

A handful of transponder tracks gave a more complete picture, filling in some of the blanks. A recurring destination was Ethiopia, particularly the Harar Meda Air Base, the Ethiopian military’s main air force facility, and Addis Ababa International Airport.

The Ethiopian embassies in Washington and Berlin did not return a request for comment.

The UAE and Russia are both deeply embroiled in the Sudanese civil war, but their governments support opposing sides. While Abu Dhabi supports the Rapid Support Forces, Russia has thrown its weight behind the government and its Sudanese Armed Forces. Aviacon Zitotrans’s apparent work for both the UAE and Russia has led to the situation that the same aircraft may be supplying opposing sides of the brutal civil war, sometimes flying from Russia and Turkey into Port Sudan, the SAF’s main supply point, and sometimes operating on UAE missions likely supporting the RSF through the African hinterland.

Aside from Africa, a handful of flights that took place during these aircraft’s apparent use by the UAE connected the Emirates to other Gulf countries, including Kuwait and Qatar.

Beyond the use of Aviacon Zitotrans aircraft, the UAE operates a fleet of cargo aircraft using front companies and ostensibly civilian charter cargo aircraft on similar missions, which Defense News will explore in a forthcoming investigation.

It’s unclear why UAE leaders picked Aviacon Zitotrans from the extensive market of cargo charter airlines. “It may be that they have seen Aviacon Zitotrans’s experience in this area, that they’ve worked in the same kind of high-sensitivity operations,” said Garcia.

The aircraft were also tracked flying other missions in equatorial and sub-Saharan Africa, including in Libya, Uganda, D.R. Congo and Nigeria, over the past year and a half. However, based on known patterns, many of these missions are likely to have been Russia-linked rather than on behalf of the UAE, even though the UAE was sometimes used as a stopover location or hub on the way.

Defense News has previously reported on an Aviacon Zitotrans Il-76 aircraft flying a secretive mission to Venezuela during mounting U.S. pressure on the country in October 2025. It was later revealed that the aircraft had delivered a Russian air defense system to Caracas. Intermediary refuelling stops are essential for these aircraft to cover such distances, as the range of the Ilyushin planes would otherwise be insufficient, the CEO of a different Russian shadow airline told Defense News as part of an earlier investigation.

“If this is the case that Aviacon is also running missions for the UAE alongside illicit missions for Russia, then it is significant because it shows that the UAE does not see the sanctions against Aviacon as a sufficient deterrent to stop working with them,” Garcia concluded.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: Conclusion of the Global Coalition’s military mission in Iraq
items.summary: UK-Iraqi security cooperation is set to enter a new phase, as the Global Coalition's military mission against Daesh in Iraq, Operation Inherent Resolve, successfully concludes and its forces - including UK personnel - depart.
items.body:
UK-Iraqi security cooperation is set to enter a new phase, as the Global Coalition’s military mission against Daesh in Iraq, Operation Inherent Resolve, successfully concludes and its forces - including UK personnel - depart.

Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country’s security.

As part of the transition to new security arrangements led by the Government of Iraq, Coalition forces, including UK personnel, have departed.

The ISF has bolstered security across Iraq, enabling the return of essential services and supporting the recovery of communities affected by conflict. With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security cooperation under Iraqi leadership.

The UK will continue to support Iraq’s security and stability, working closely with Iraqi partners to develop an enduring bilateral defence partnership.

Operation Inherent Resolve was established in 2014 to advise, assist and enable partner forces to secure the lasting defeat of Daesh and establish enduring security cooperation. This mission operates under The Global Coalition Against Daesh, consisting of 90 partners.

During the last decade, the UK has played a leading role through Operation SHADER, the UK’s contribution to Operation Inherent Resolve. At the invitation of the Iraqi government, UK forces provided valuable support, training and assistance to more than 111,000 members of the ISF, including more than 21,000 of the Peshmerga, in crucial infantry, weapons maintenance, counter-IED, medical and engineering skills.

The RAF has also conducted thousands of sorties striking more than 2300 Daesh targets, as well as providing critical surveillance and reconnaissance in support of ISF ground operations.

We pay tribute to the UK personnel who have played their part in the Global Coalition. Working alongside our global Coalition partners, the UK remains committed to ensuring the global defeat of Daesh and its violent ideology including through the continuation of Operation SHADER. Alongside security partnerships, the UK will continue to lead the coordination of Coalition communications that counter Daesh propaganda and build resilience against terrorist messaging.

Our commitment to Iraq and the wider region remains steadfast. Building on a decade of close cooperation, we look forward to developing an enduring bilateral defence partnership with Iraq. This will focus on counter-terrorism cooperation, military education, capability development, defence industrial collaboration and advancing our shared security interests.

items.title: Accountability and Alignment Strategies for Implementing Edtech
items.author: Alice Huguet
items.summary: The authors use two concepts from educational policy literature, accountability and alignment, to examine strategies that a school district implemented to spur the increased usage of an educational technology platform for learning math.
items.body:
How One School District Narrowed the Gap Between Promise and Practice

ResearchPublished Sep 30, 2026

This research was sponsored by the Institute of Education Sciences.

In this report, the authors describe the strategies that one district and its schools used during a two-year period in which the number of students meeting usage goals in Zearn Math, a mathematics educational technology platform, more than doubled. The authors use two concepts from implementation research, accountability and alignment, to examine the district- and school-level strategies associated with this increased usage.

Educational technology (edtech) products are central in many school districts’ instructional strategies. However, prior research shows that school districts often struggle to move from adopting edtech products to ensuring that students use them consistently. Students’ and schools’ use of edtech products often fall below developer-recommended levels. But what if a district could meaningfully narrow the gap between recommended and actual use?

In this report, the authors describe the strategies that one district and its schools used during a two-year period in which usage of Zearn Math, a mathematics edtech platform, increased markedly. The authors draw on a randomized controlled trial in which 32 schools in a large, urban school district supplemented math instruction for grades three through five with Zearn Math. In the study’s first year, fewer than one in five students met the platform’s annual lesson goal. In the second year, about half did.

Zooming in on qualitative data from six case study treatment schools, the authors use two concepts from implementation research, accountability and alignment, to examine the district- and school-level strategies associated with this increased usage. They found that clear expectations, monitoring, and incentives helped prioritize Zearn Math’s usage. Such strategies as better alignment between the platform and primary curriculum, dedicated usage time, fewer competing tools, and expanded professional learning opportunities made using Zearn Math easier for teachers. The authors also discuss trade-offs, including that, while most participating teachers found these strategies to be helpful, others reported that they might have displaced other valuable learning activities.

- These strategies included setting clearer expectations, centralizing usage monitoring, and offering incentives for individual students, classrooms, and schools.

- These strategies included improved alignment between Zearn Math and the district’s core math curriculum, dedicated time for platform use in school schedules, fewer competing products, and expanded professional learning.

- A spring incentive campaign in year two appeared to build on the expectations, scheduled time, and monitoring that were already in place. Interviewees often referred to these shifts in conjunction with one another—more as a package than as independent components.

- Although many teachers welcomed the added clarity and structure, some described the new expectations in year two as stressful, worried about consequences for not meeting targets, or questioned whether time spent on the platform displaced other valued activities.

- District and school leaders should clearly and consistently communicate expectations for edtech implementation.

- District and school leaders should consider using incentives at the school, classroom, and student levels to build buy-in.

- District and school leaders should plan professional learning that specifically supports a platform’s or product’s implementation.

- District leaders should preserve space for school- and classroom-level decisionmaking within implementation guidance.

- District leaders should evaluate whether edtech products fit with the primary curriculum so that time on the platform supports their overall learning objectives.

- District leaders should monitor progress toward edtech implementation goals using both quantitative data (e.g., the number of lessons completed) and qualitative feedback (e.g., results from teacher surveys or school leader check-ins).

- School leaders should ensure that edtech expectations align with other teacher guidance to avoid contradictory messages about priorities.

- School leaders should explore options for allocating dedicated time for edtech use in the school schedule.

- School leaders should explicitly connect edtech with the school’s instructional vision to help teachers understand how the edtech product supports students’ learning goals.

items.title: Veterans Support to Self-Reliance Pilot Program
items.author: Sarah B. Hunter
items.summary: This report presents findings from the impact evaluation of California’s Veterans Support to Self-Reliance initiative, which is designed to provide enhanced supportive services to veterans living in permanent supportive housing.
items.body:
Final Evaluation Report

ResearchPublished Sep 30, 2026

This research was made possible by a grant from Swords to Plowshares.

This report presents findings from the impact evaluation of California’s Veterans Support to Self-Reliance initiative, which is designed to provide enhanced supportive services to veterans living in permanent supportive housing. The authors documenting trends in service utilization and well-being outcomes, including health-related behaviors, health care utilization, social support and connectedness, and perceived quality of life.

California’s Veterans Support to Self-Reliance pilot kept formerly homeless veterans housed at a fraction of the cost of nursing facilities or assisted living—and their health outcomes improved.

More than 9,000 veterans experienced homelessness in California in 2024, and roughly 69 percent of the state's veteran population is 55 or older. Veterans who have experienced chronic homelessness often arrive in permanent supportive housing (PSH) with serious health and functional challenges that standard subsidies and case management may not fully address.

In 2023, the California Department of Veterans Affairs (CalVet) launched the Veterans Support to Self-Reliance (VSSR) pilot at 13 PSH locations across six counties. RAND researchers evaluated whom the pilot reached, how participants fared over three years, and what it cost relative to alternatives.

Only 20 of 560 participants exited to an unstable situation over three years—an adverse exit rate of 3.6 percent, compared with 15 percent reported for a comparable veteran population.

Falls fell 59 percent, emergency medical visits fell 75 percent, and the share of residents with no acute events rose from 74 to 90 percent.

Missed medical appointments fell 54 percent, the share eating three meals daily rose from 37 to 53 percent, and alcohol, stimulant, and opioid use each fell 40 percent or more.

Total public investment ran roughly $42,800 to $66,200 per veteran per year—23 to 50 percent below assisted living and between one-quarter and just under one-half the cost of semi-private nursing facility care.

- Prioritize peer support specialist and service assistant roles in any continuation or successor program; all four grantees rated these highest-value, and the group programming they enable is associated with fewer habitability complaints and more time outside residents’ units.

- Close remaining unmet need in housekeeping, which was reported by 13 percent of residents at the end of their first year, along with meal preparation and laundry, each near 7 percent.

- To enable a future causal evaluation, establish a data linkage with the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs and regional Homeless Management Information Systems to build a propensity-matched comparison group of veterans who did not receive VSSR services.

- Report VSSR’s negative exit rate against published Continuum of Care benchmarks, noting that exit destination data can be unreliable.

RAND researchers analyzed program data from 560 veterans enrolled in the VSSR pilot between June 2023 and May 2026. The evaluation included descriptive analysis of participant characteristics and housing exits; mixed-effects models linking quarterly service use to health and housing outcomes; and paired survey comparisons tracking self-rated quality of life, health, and housing conditions over time. Researchers also estimated annual cost per veteran using grantee expenditure data and compared those figures with California residential care alternatives. Semistructured interviews with leadership at all four grantee organizations and a structured review of 16 evaluations of housing interventions informed recommendations for a future causal evaluation.

items.title: Can AGI Rivals Hold Back?
items.author: Alvin Moon
items.summary: With this analysis, the authors identify the conditions under which restraint is feasible and sustainable, as well as show how these conditions shift as states come to believe that they are close to attaining artificial general intelligence.
items.body:
Without domestic AI oversight, rivals can’t credibly commit to restraint—even when both sides want to.

The race to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI) poses a familiar strategic dilemma: Each rival might prefer that everyone hold back, but none can be sure the others will. Any restraint arrangement depends on verification—and verification depends on whether states have built the domestic institutions that make their own artificial intelligence (AI) ecosystems legible.

RAND researchers developed a game-theoretic model to identify the conditions under which mutual restraint is feasible and self-enforcing. They examine how domestic oversight, the detectability of cheating, proximity to AGI arrival, and fears of catastrophe interact to determine whether restraint between rivals can hold.

Domestic AI oversight can enable international restraint.

- A state that hasn’t made its AI industry transparent—even to itself—can’t prove it’s complying with a restraint arrangement.

Fear of catastrophe deters some cheating, but not all.

- A state that expects to share in the catastrophic risk it creates by defecting is partly self-deterred. But deterring purely positional defections—those aimed at reaching AGI first—requires detection.

Verification loses force as AGI arrival appears imminent.

- As rivals come to believe AGI is near, the remaining time to punish defectors shrinks. Only instruments tied to post-AGI outcomes may still deter cheating.

Mutual doubt can trap rivals in an opaque world.

- Even if preferable, restraint may still fail when one rival doubts that the other will make its actions verifiable. Building the means for verification enables states to choose mutual restraint.

To preserve the option of mutual restraint, states should:

- Treat domestic AI governance—compute registries, licensing, facility audits, and incident reporting—as security architecture, not just regulation, because it creates the evidentiary foundation that restraint arrangements require.

- Invest in verification technologies that do not expose sensitive information, such as confidential-computing and trusted-hardware methods, to lower the security cost of demonstrating compliance to a rival.

- Develop instruments that tie post-AGI outcomes to pre-AGI conduct before they are needed, while detection-backed punishment can still reinforce them.

- Consider reducing a rival’s cost of building oversight capacity through technical assistance or shared monitoring platforms: The feasibility of mutual restraint is determined by whichever rival finds transparency more costly.

RAND researchers developed a two-stage game-theoretic model to analyze the conditions under which rival states can sustain mutual restraint in AGI development without being able to directly observe the other’s compliance. In Stage 1, each state chooses how much oversight to impose on its own AI industry beyond what domestic policy requires. In Stage 2, states interact repeatedly until AGI arrives, choosing whether to comply, race openly, or covertly defect in each period. The analysis draws on repeated game theory, arms control literature, and prior RAND research on the strategic dynamics of AGI competition.

items.title: DAF awards F-15EX Lot 7 contract for 22 aircraft
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: Program negotiators successfully navigated inflation and earlier production disruptions to maintain the full 22-aircraft buy before the fiscal year-end deadline.
items.body:
Published Sept. 29, 2026

Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate

The Department of the Air Force awarded Boeing a contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II aircraft under Lot 7 — preserving the buying power of congressionally provided reconciliation funding and sustaining F-15EX production. The Lot 7 agreement accounts for current programmatic realities, including the effects of the 2025 production disruption and broader inflation across the defense industrial base. Through focused, complex negotiations, the F-15 Program Office and Boeing reached an agreement that maintains the procurement of all 22 Lot 7 aircraft within available funding. "Lot 7 reflects a disciplined approach to executing available resources while balancing the realities affecting defense production," said Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich , portfolio acquisition executive for the Fighters and Advanced Aircraft Directorate . "The team remained focused on affordability, production continuity and delivering the aircraft needed to modernize the U.S. Air Force’s fighter fleet for the threats we face today and into the future." The F-15EX is a modern, multirole heavy fighter that builds on the proven F-15 design. The aircraft incorporates advanced avionics, large-area displays, digital backbone architecture and enhanced survivability capabilities. It is intended to replace aging F-15C and F-15D aircraft while providing a platform for continued modernization as operational requirements evolve. The Lot 7 award also demonstrates the application of the Secretary of War's acquisition transformation principles by empowering an integrated F-15 negotiation team to rapidly deliver capability. The team synchronized expertise across functional areas, elevated issues requiring senior-level decisions, and maintained accountability for cost, schedule, and aircraft quantity — demonstrating the speed, disciplined execution, and mission-focused accountability central to the warfighting acquisition system. This award followed extensive collaboration among program management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management, logistics and other acquisition professionals. The team assessed the impacts of changing production conditions and inflation, aligned the aircraft procurement with available funding, and completed the action before the fiscal-year deadline. Senior department leaders supported timely coordination and decision-making throughout the process. Their engagement enabled the team to address complex affordability and execution challenges while maintaining focus on the program’s operational purpose: delivering modern fighter capability to Airmen. "The Lot 7 award demonstrates what is possible when the acquisition enterprise moves with purpose, remains accountable to the taxpayer and stays focused on delivering capability to the warfighter," said Col. Jonathan Varoli, system program manager of the directorate's F-15 Program Office. "This effort brought together the right expertise, at the right time, to achieve an outcome that strengthens the F-15EX program and supports the future fighter force." The Department of the Air Force will continue working with Boeing to support rapid, affordable and sustainable F-15EX production. The Lot 7 award sustains the program’s near-term production effort while the Air Force continues to assess future requirements and acquisition strategies.

items.title: Air Force advances point defense enterprise with plans for new weapon system, career field
items.author: Pentagon News
items.summary: The U.S. Air Force is advancing point defense as a core function of air and space power, strengthening its ability to protect the Airmen, aircraft, infrastructure and other critical assets required to generate combat airpower.
items.body:
Published Sept. 29, 2026

Secretary of the Air Force Public Affairs

The U.S. Air Force is advancing point defense as a core function of air and space power, strengthening its ability to protect the Airmen, aircraft, infrastructure and other critical assets required to generate combat airpower. Chief of Staff of the Air Force Gen. Ken Wilsbach announced two related initiatives during his Sept. 14 keynote address at the 2026 Air and Space Forces Association Air, Space & Cyber Conference: establishment of the Point Defense Weapon System and development of a dedicated career field for point defense Airmen. “Ultimately, point defense is about preserving our ability to generate combat airpower,” Lt. Gen. Case Cunningham , Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations, said. “We’re building the Airmen, the systems and the integrated command and control necessary to keep our bases operating and our aircraft flying in the face of attack.” The Point Defense Weapon System will be an integrated system-of-systems designed to connect sensors, command and control and layered kinetic and non-kinetic capabilities to detect, track and defeat airborne threats before they can disrupt installation operations. Rather than a single platform, the weapon system will provide an enterprise-wide framework capable of integrating new capabilities as threats, technologies and operational requirements evolve. Point defense is an established military concept focused on protecting specific areas or critical assets from attack. The Air Force’s April 2025 “ Point Defense of Air Bases Doctrine Advisory ,” which builds on existing Air Force and joint doctrine, describes how installation-level defensive capabilities complement and integrate with the broader joint air and missile defense architecture. The Air Force also plans to establish a new career field of point defense Airmen, with the goal of becoming operational within two years. These Airmen will develop specialized expertise in operating and integrating sensors, command and control, and layered defensive capabilities. They will work alongside Security Forces and other Air Force and joint mission partners to deliver coordinated and layered defense of installations. “Establishing a new career field is about more than creating a specialty code,” Lt. Gen. Jefferson O’Donnell , Air Force deputy chief of staff for manpower, personnel and services, said. “We must build a professional community with the right training, experience, and career development to deliver this capability over time. Success is an Air Force where Airmen—recruited, trained, developed, and retained as point defense specialists—strengthen the Air Force's ability to fight and win.” The effort builds upon the Air Force’s established integrated defense approach, which brings together installation capabilities to protect personnel, resources and combat operations. Security Forces provide essential expertise in planning and executing integrated defense, while the new career field will add dedicated expertise to help integrate point defense capabilities into the broader defensive architecture. “Our Security Forces Airmen have built a legacy of excellence in integrated defense,” Lt. Gen. Kenyon Bell , Air Force deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering and force protection, said. “They understand how to bring capabilities together to protect our installations and keep the mission going. Point defense builds on that foundation, integrating our defenders with specialized point defense forces to create an even more effective, layered defense.” To strengthen integration between the two career fields, a Security Forces Airman will serve as deputy career field manager for point defense, helping to align training, professional development and operational expertise across both communities. The point defense enterprise must also integrate beyond the installation. In the homeland, these capabilities will connect with existing air defense arrangements and operate within applicable airspace and engagement authorities. During contingency operations and conflict, they will integrate with the theater’s joint air and missile defense architecture, ensuring local defensive capabilities contribute to, and benefit from, the broader air picture. “Defense of our air bases cannot occur in isolation from the airspace around them,” Lt. Gen. Case Cunningham, Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations, said. “Our sensors, command and control and defensive tools must connect to the broader air defense network, whether we’re defending an installation in the homeland or a forward operating location in conflict. We need to contribute to that larger picture and benefit from what the joint force sees, giving commanders the information and options they need to employ the right effect at the right time.” The Point Defense Weapon System is being designed to evolve rapidly as new technologies emerge and operating environments change. “We need a weapon system that can adapt as quickly as the threat,” said Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi , Air Force deputy chief of staff for force modernization and chief modernization officer. “That means building an open, modular architecture that allows us to rapidly integrate new sensors and defensive tools, adapt to different operating environments and remain connected to the broader defensive network.” The Air Force is in the early stages of developing both the Point Defense Weapon System and career field. Additional implementation details will be announced as the service refines requirements, training, force development and integration plans.

items.title: Evaluation of U.S. Policies to Increase Domestic Access to Critical Minerals
items.author: Tom Blaubach
items.summary: The United States has launched a wide-ranging industrial policy effort to secure the domestic supply of critical minerals. In this report, the authors describe the relative strengths and weaknesses of several of the policy tools used in that effort.
items.body:
Every U.S. policy tool for securing access to critical minerals involves trade-offs. Knowing which tool fits which problem will allow the government to better design and apply policies going forward.

China controls more than 70 percent of the world’s supply of several critical minerals, and it has shown a willingness to weaponize that dominance through export controls. The resulting price spikes and supply uncertainty threaten the United States—particularly its defense, energy, and manufacturing sectors.

The U.S. government has responded with a set of policy tools, such as tax credits, loans, stockpiles, import tariffs, and permitting reforms. But which tools actually work, and for whom? RAND researchers analyzed each tool using economic theory and historical examples, as well as structured interviews with industry representatives across the critical mineral value chain.

Stockpiling is the only fast path to resilience.

Every other policy tool examined takes years to significantly strengthen the U.S. critical mineral supply chain. Stockpiling can deliver results within months, depending on design.

Most policies undercut investment in substitutes.

Policies that boost domestic production tend to lower prices, which reduces the economic incentive to develop alternative materials or technologies that could reduce U.S. dependence in the long term.

Policy design and implementation both matter.

Uncertainty, lack of transparency, and slow timelines make otherwise sound policy tools less effective. Industry representatives cited these process failures as major deterrents to investment.

Needs differ sharply across the value chain.

For example, miners need permitting certainty before capital support, but smelters and refiners need multiple forms of stacked support to overcome structurally thin margins.

For federal interagency bodies coordinating the critical mineral policy effort:

- Make all critical mineral programs competitive and open to qualified applicants, using objective and transparent eligibility criteria.

- Improve the accessibility and transparency of capital support programs.

- Stop making equity investments in critical mineral producers; low-cost debt achieves similar goals without the governance complications and ownership dilution.

- Extend production tax credits indefinitely; their value depends on durability, and industry will not plan around credits that may disappear before projects reach production.

- Streamline permitting pathways and reduce litigation risk.

- Limit import tariffs to materials with at least some existing domestic production capacity to avoid raising costs for downstream manufacturers.

- Include producer countries in plurilateral trade agreements to secure affordable feedstock access for U.S. refiners until domestic mining capacity expands.

- Match policy tools to the specific market segment and commodity.

RAND researchers used a two-part approach. First, they evaluated each policy tool against five economic criteria—effects on domestic production capacity, incentives for substitutes and efficiency improvements, effects on downstream industries, the speed of impact, and budget effects—drawing on economic theory and historical U.S. industrial policy experience. Next, they conducted structured interviews with 16 representatives from firms across the critical mineral value chain, including miners, smelters, refiners, financiers, and innovation companies. Interview responses were coded against predefined categories and analyzed by value chain segment, company size, and commodity market size to identify patterns in barriers and policy preferences.

items.title: Novel effectors
items.author: James Black
items.summary: This project examines how maturing novel effectors, including hypersonics, directed energy, cyber, electromagnetic and autonomous systems, affect strategic stability, international governance and the United Kingdom's strategic position.
items.body:
A raft of ‘novel effector’ technologies are maturing at pace. Some, such as hypersonic missiles, are already in operational use. Others, such as Directed Energy Weapons (DEWs) are on the cusp of more regular deployment. The landscape for these technologies is fast-moving, and accelerating, but the strategic implications of these technologies are poorly understood. This impacts international governance and stability, and the UK’s relative positioning in these technologies.

This project, commissioned by the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), explores the strategic stability implications of so-called ‘novel effector’ technologies in the defence context. It defines the novel effector technologies of most strategic concern and charts their development trajectories across major actors. Using a strategic cultures lens of analysis, it then considers relative perceptions of their use across major actors before considering options for their international governance based on the most pressing gaps and risks, before assessing opportunities for the UK.

Novel effector technologies are complex to categorise and have varied implications, but they share three strategic implications. Focusing on hypersonics, directed energy weapons, cyber, autonomous & electromagnetic pulse, we identified three core common characteristics. Each of these technologies can compress decision-making timescales, reduce attributability and proliferate widely. These risks are heightened by divergent assumptions among major actors about how such may be used. In some contexts, non-nuclear systems could also be perceived as threatening nuclear command and control, creating escalation risks.

Prospects for binding international governance in these technologies are found to be limited, given low convergence between major actors on the technologies’ intended uses and acceptable constraints. However, targeted transparency and confidence-building measures could help manage the most acute risks: miscalculation and inadvertent escalation for hypersonics and DEWs; and ambiguity over civilian infrastructure, legitimate targets and human oversight for autonomous, cyber and electromagnetic effectors.

The UK also has competitive opportunities in this technology space. The UK’s defence research and development (R&D) base and strengths in DEWs and selected hypersonic sub-systems create scope for targeted leadership. A selective approach would prioritise sovereign ownership where essential, collaboration with allies where advantageous, and assured access to fast-moving innovations where partnership is the most efficient route.

items.title: The Scope and Nature of the U.S.-China Competition
items.author: Anne Stickells
items.summary: This is the first of several reports in a RAND study on the U.S.-China competition. The authors provide a framework for evaluating the character and status of that competition and give insight into how the United States can gain strategic leverage.
items.body:
Significant debates remain underway on some of the most essential aspects of the U.S. contest with China: the nature of the competitor, the main elements of the competition, a sense of what the competition is truly about, what success looks like, and a theory of success to bring about that end. What is clear is that the United States is dealing with a rival whose dynamism derives not from ideological expansion but from economic development, a growing influence in international institutions and processes, and an increasingly strong position in the fields of science and technology.

The competition is clearly something other than a classic power transition; China is rising relative to the United States but not in a straight-line trajectory. China is not set to dominate world politics. Although China is immense and influential, its horizons are not infinite, and its power is counterbalanced by a variety of factors.

This report is the first of several deliverables in a RAND study on U.S.-China competition, and in this report, the authors offer a clear framework for understanding the elements of the competition and placing that framework in a broader conception of the competition’s nature. To build such a conceptualization, the authors reviewed U.S. and Chinese concepts of national power and statecraft and reexamined earlier RAND research on competition. The authors share their findings and deliver initial recommendations for how the United States can devise a strategy to counter China and gain strategic leverage in the competition.

items.title: Future C2 and Counter-C2 systems
items.author: James Black
items.summary: This study examines how emerging non-nuclear command and control and counter-C2 systems could affect strategic stability as digital technology, AI, commercial infrastructure and contested information transform military operations and decisions.
items.body:
Implications for strategic stability of developments in non-nuclear command and control

ResearchPublished Sep 29, 2026

This research was sponsored by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).

Effective command and control supports situational awareness and military direction, but digitalisation, AI, commercial infrastructure and contested information are increasing complexity and vulnerability. Commissioned by the UK FCDO, this study examines how emerging non-nuclear C2 and counter-C2 systems could affect strategic stability, including risks of miscalculation, pre-emption and escalation, and considers how governance may mitigate them.

Effective command and control (C2) enables armed forces to maintain situational awareness and direct operations across assessment, planning, preparation and execution. However, C2 is becoming more complex as digital, commercial and operational trends interact. Expanding computing and telecommunications infrastructure permits large-scale data collection and analysis, but much of it is civilian-owned and outside Defence’s direct control. Advances in machine learning can rapidly identify patterns and suggest courses of action, while misinformation, disinformation and AI-generated content make reliable information harder to distinguish from noise. Increasingly integrated operational domains and multi-domain operations also challenge command models designed around a single geographic area.

Although individual trends affecting C2 have been studied, their combined implications for strategic stability—and the scope for governance to mitigate associated risks—remain insufficiently understood. Commissioned by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), this study examines how developments in non-nuclear C2 and counter-C2 systems may affect strategic stability. Here, C2 means the processes through which orders, guidance and direction are given to force elements. Strategic stability is understood as a security condition in which no state believes it can gain a decisive advantage through force, including a first strike or conflict escalation.

- AI, advanced sensing, synthetic environments and human–machine teaming can increase operational tempo, but connectivity expands cyber and physical attack surfaces, dependence on data and the risk of crisis miscalculation.

- Technology alone is insufficient: legacy systems, siloed data, procurement and organisational culture require corresponding changes to structures, skills and practices.

- Commercial cloud, satellite and communications infrastructure supports resilience, yet introduces actors, incentives and vulnerabilities beyond Defence’s control, complicating attribution, accountability and crisis management.

- Trustworthy information and human judgement remain essential. Manipulation, poor-quality data and over-reliance on automation can erode transparency and professional judgement; personnel must challenge machine outputs and operate through degradation.

- Distributed C2 can improve deterrence, but commercial dependence, opaque automation and faster decisions may create uncertainty about survivability and incentives for pre-emption or escalation.

- Counter-C2 tools—including cyber-attacks, jamming, counterspace operations and strikes on key nodes—may favour disruption over control because they are accessible and hard to attribute. Redundancy can limit effects.

- Divergent C2 cultures—distributed authority and human oversight versus centralised, automated chains—can cause states to misread intentions.

- Soft governance is the most practical means of reducing risk: shared research, experimentation, interoperability standards, industry engagement and crisis communications can build trust and address vulnerabilities before practices become entrenched.

- The FCDO and wider UK government should promote international cooperation on emerging C2 technologies through shared research, experimentation, confidence-building measures and reliable crisis communications. With the MOD, NATO and partners, they should advance interoperable data standards and interfaces while preserving national sovereignty.

- Defence should strengthen cybersecurity, data validation and information assurance; keep human judgement central to AI-enabled decisions; and train personnel for contested and degraded environments.

- Government and industry should map critical commercial dependencies, build redundancy and joint incident-response arrangements, and improve civilian–military coordination through shared playbooks, routine information exchange and joint planning. These measures should inform procurement and alliance planning.

items.title: Adversarial artificial intelligence
items.author: William Mitchell Reid
items.summary: As military AI use grows, attacks that disrupt or deny AI systems could threaten strategic stability. This study examines risks to military and critical infrastructure systems, and recommends measures to reduce attacks and their impact globally.
items.body:
Implications of strategic stability attacks on military AI systems

ResearchPublished Sep 29, 2026

This research was sponsored by the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO).

Strategic competition in military AI is intensifying, but governance has not kept pace. As reliance on AI-enabled decision making grows, adversarial attacks that disrupt, deny or manipulate military and critical infrastructure systems could undermine strategic stability. This study examines how such attacks may affect credibility, escalation, trust and attribution, and recommends measures to reduce their likelihood and impact worldwide.

Strategic competition in artificial intelligence (AI), including in the military domain, is intensifying, while global governance has not kept pace. The tactical implications of military AI are well documented: autonomous targeting, navigation in robotic systems, and decision-support tools for commanders are relatively well understood. Growing attention is now directed toward AI’s strategic effects and its influence on strategic stability.

Although research on the strategic implications of AI and governance options is expanding, it largely focuses on the potential benefits of effective AI systems. Little attention has been paid to how the disruption or denial of AI systems could threaten strategic stability. As a result, governance proposals rarely address these risks. Yet as AI is increasingly integrated in decision making and reliance on these systems grows, the consequences of adversarial interference will likewise intensify.

This project, commissioned by the UK Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), offers insights into how adversarial AI attacks targeting AI systems integrated in the military or critical national infrastructure may affect strategic stability, and offers recommendations to decrease the probability and impact of adversarial attacks on AI systems.

- The (perceived) vulnerability of AI systems to adversarial attacks undermines the credibility of defence to adversaries and allies.

- Adversarial AI may tip the offence-defence balance in favour of the offence.

- Ambiguity, distinguishing ‘normal’ AI malfunction due to model fragility and deliberate adversarial attacks, and the difficulty of attribution create opportunities for miscalculation and mistrust. Empowerment of non-state actors through democratisation of technology, and specifically adversarial AI, further complicates attribution.

- Entanglement of conventional and nuclear C3 increases the risk of an accidental attack on NC3, risking escalation.

- Governments should treat adversarial AI as a strategic stability risk, not merely a cyber security or AI assurance issue. They should incorporate these risks into national governance and international forums; share threat information with allies, incidents, attribution and emerging techniques; review significant incidents; and develop expertise across foreign policy, defence, security, cyber and assurance communities. They should strengthen AI-enabled military systems, nuclear and dual-use command, control and communications, and critical infrastructure through robust design, resilience, recovery planning and fallback options. Clear red lines, response options and communication channels with competitors are also needed to reduce miscalculation, mistrust and escalation risks.

items.title: Evaluating the UK Government’s 10-year drug strategy
items.author: Carol Black
items.summary: Dame Carol Black, Lucy Strang, and Jennifer Newbould discuss RAND Europe’s evaluation of the first three years of implementation of the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio as part of the UK government’s 10-year drug strategy, From Harm to Hope.
items.body:
D-SITAR Methods Report

Apr 22, 2026

The captions for this video are auto-generated and have not been edited.

VideoPublished Sep 28, 2026

Dame Carol Black, Lucy Strang, and Jennifer Newbould discuss RAND Europe’s evaluation of the first three years of implementation of the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio as part of the UK government’s 10-year drug strategy. While the funding has been a welcome boost and there is wide support for the Portfolio’s aims, it has not yet achieved a world-class treatment system and a whole-system approach to alcohol and/or other drugs.

Dame Carol Black

It seems to me it's extremely important - I know there are lots of other very, very important things going on - but if you want better health and you want a safer society, you need to pay attention to drugs.

In 2021, drug-related deaths in the UK were the highest ever recorded. Dame Carol Black's independent review of drugs found that drugs cost an estimated £19bn to society annually and that long-term cuts in funding have led to a decline in skills, expertise and capacity in the treatment and recovery system.

My review of drugs was commissioned by the then Home Secretary who was Sajid Javid and he asked me to do it in two parts. The first part was to really look at the evidence of where we were with the drug scene and with addiction. Wherever you looked, it didn't matter which part of the drug agenda you looked at, we were in a bad place.

In response to the issue, the UK government published their 10-year drug strategy From Harm to Hope. This strategy included an additional £780m in funding over three years for the treatment and recovery system.

So over the past two-and-a-half years, RAND Europe and our partners have evaluated the first three years of the drug strategy's Treatment and Recovery Portfolio implementation in England. We evaluated the Portfolio as a whole, as well as focusing in on five priority areas which are the housing support grant, efforts to improve the treatment and recovery workforce, lived-experience recovery organisations, the integration of mental and physical health services and the provision of depot buprenorphine, which is a long-lasting medication used for opioid substitution therapy in the recovery process. So the workforce within the treatment and recovery sector was obviously a key priority of this additional investment. There was a widespread recognition that, after years of disinvestment, the state of the workforce had been depleted and it was a real challenge to build that up over time, specifically within the planned timelines of the Portfolio.

Our findings suggest that it's not necessarily the nature of the work that leads people to leave the sector, but other factors such as salary levels, job security, workload and the availability of resources. All these things are amenable to change and are what ultimately affect people's desire to continue in the treatment and recovery sector.

Another key priority of the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio was to improve mental and physical health service integration. So it's really critical for people who use treatment and recovery services to also have really well-integrated support from both mental and physical health services. This is because a lot of their needs are also extending to other mental health challenges or physical health needs and we do find that these individuals can often fall through the cracks between these services.

So we've now got three more years of money. And if I had to concentrate now it would be on absolutely addressing the quality issue: the quality of the workforce, the quality of what is done in the treatment areas really being more sophisticated and person-centred about delivery.

What we found through our evaluations was a few really important steps that the government should take in ensuring that the Treatment and Recovery Portfolio meets its intended aims and continues to provide really good outcomes for people who are using these services and for people who are working in the sector. First of all, we recommended that the government continue to provide more funding security to really ensure that the full 10 years of the Portfolio will be recognised and realised.

So the funding was well received, but in many areas people felt that it just replaced years of disinvestment. If we don't invest in people who use drugs and alcohol now, the problem will only get larger in the future.

We also really emphasised the importance of continuing to make progress with mental and physical health service integration to ensure that people who are using these services have all their needs addressed in a really collaborative and cohesive way.

We have failed so far to get drug addiction considered a chronic health condition and given the parity of a health condition. We haven't succeeded to improve the physical complications that drug-dependent people suffer from.

We also found that there is more work to be done in ensuring a whole-system approach to dealing with drug issues. So that involves work and collaboration across multiple sectors including health, education, employment, criminal justice and so on.

I would say please empower your local delivery services to be brave, to be less bureaucratic and to deliver a person-centred service. These are individuals with complex problems and they needed not to be treated as a number, a form-filling exercise. They need to be treated as a person with a chronic health condition, given some choice and able to go along a journey which will lead to recovery.

items.title: Counterterror and Great Power Competition in the Sahel
items.author: Sean M. Zeigler
items.summary: This study develops a game-theoretic model to explain why jihadist expansion has strained traditional Western partnerships and encouraged governments to seek Russian assistance.
items.body:
ResearchPosted on rand.org Sep 28, 2026Published in: Defence and Peace Economics, Volume 37, Issue 6, pages 960-980 (2026). DOI: 10.1080/10242694.2026.2687488

The Sahel has become the epicenter of global terrorism, accounting for half of all terrorism-related fatalities by 2024. Jihadist groups pursuing system-transforming agendas have expanded across the region by aligning with local militant actors and building durable insurgencies. Their growth has disrupted longstanding security relationships between Sahelian governments and France, the United States, and the United Kingdom, with many of these new states reorienting and seeking security support from Russia. This study develops a game-theoretic model to explain why jihadist expansion has strained traditional Western partnerships and encouraged governments to seek Russian assistance. We also present an alternative model demonstrating how negotiated settlements can reduce jihadist appeal and limit external rival influence. We show that jihadist groups enhance local militants’ capabilities, reducing prospects for negotiated settlements with host states. At the same time, jihadist intervention increases the political and military costs borne by Western partners, weakening their capacity to sustain long-term security commitments. These dynamics create opportunities for Russia to expand its influence by offering security services through mercenary forces that profit from ongoing conflict. We conclude that arming host states is likely to prolong conflict, whereas negotiation and peace aid can isolate jihadist groups and promote a more stable peace.

items.body:
DAYTON, Ohio (AFLCMC) -- “You are part of the fight,” Lt. Gen. Jason Voorheis, commander of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center (AFLCMC) told attendees at the Ohio Defense and Aerospace Forum earlier this week. “ General Dale White [Director, Critical Major Weapon Systems at the Pentagon] is fond of saying that militaries don't go to war - nations go to war. You all are part of what our nation brings to the fight in terms of developing fielding and getting capability into the hands of our warfighters.”

Voorheis spoke as part of a panel titled “Power Projection from the Heartland.” He was joined on stage by Brig. Gen. Timothy Helfrich, AFLCMC Portfolio Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Fighters and Advanced Aircraft, alongside defense industry professionals TK Kubit and Anthony Cain. JP Nauseef of JobsOhio moderated the discussion. The forum was hosted by the Dayton Development Coalition.

Held at Wright State University on September 21, 2026, the forum highlighted the strategic alignment between Air Force modernization priorities and the Ohio defense ecosystem.

Acquisition Speed and Agility

The Ohio Defense Ecosystem

Workforce and Talent Development

In his opening remarks, Voorheis explained the Air Force acquisition workforce's shift to accept risk earlier, lean into commercial technology and open mission systems, and empower program teams to make decisions that drive projects forward.

Both Voorheis and Helfrich noted that acquisition teams at Wright-Patt and across the Center are transitioning away from platform-specific "stovepipes" to focus on broader, integrated capabilities across advanced aircraft. These teams are also balancing intensive current fleet modernization with future systems development by shifting from individual platform upgrades to an integrated, "system of systems" approach.

“I think one of the really important parts about the acquisition transformation is the change in philosophy and focus on delivering fielded capability as kind of the preeminent prioritized pacing thing that we do, and everything else is about how we achieve that to include the authorities we're giving PAEs,” noted Voorheis.

Helfrich’s Fighters and Advanced Aircraft portfolio includes the A-10, F-15, F-16, F-22, plus the FQ-42, FQ-44, other collaborative combat aircraft.

The Air Force Research Lab (AFRL) is also headquartered at Wright-Patt. Helfrich touted how AFRL led key advances in open architecture and credits AFRL with developing the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program.

“There would be no CCA without the Air Force Research Laboratory,” explained Helfrich. “Both the FQ-42 Vengeance [and] the FQ-44 Fury were heavily invested in by AFRL. Because software is sold separately with CCA, the mission autonomy work started at AFRL. They were really the ones who put together the first consortium to build Autonomous Government Reference Architecture (A-GRA). This has become a huge program, all made possible because of the investments by AFRL.”

For both Voorheis and Helfrich, the workforce and supporting infrastructure remain top concerns. Helfrich urged educators in the audience to modernize military engineering and software development classes. Both speakers noted the shortage of physical defense infrastructure in the area around Wright-Patterson, particularly for high-level classified work.

In addition to physical plant limitations, hiring remains a challenge. AFLCMC currently has over 1,700 vacancies , with more than half located at Wright-Patt. Most open positions are in technical fields like engineering and logistics. Business areas like contracting and program management also have many openings.

“We need help recruiting from the universities and from industry as well, both defense industry and non-defense industry,” explained Voorheis. “You don't have to come in with a lot of aerospace experience. What we really need is highly talented, motivated, critical thinkers.”

The panel marked the first time Lt. Gen. Voorheis has publicly spoken about his role leading AFLCMC since assuming command late last month .
items.titleZh: AFLCMC司令在俄亥俄州国防与航空航天论坛上阐述采办优先事项
items.summaryZh: 俄亥俄州代顿（AFLCMC）——“你们也是这场战斗的一部分，”美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）司令Lt. Gen.贾森·沃希斯（Jason Voorheis）本周早些时候在俄亥俄州国防与航空航天论坛上对与会者表示。“Gen.戴尔·怀特（五角大楼关键重大武器系统主管）喜欢说，参战的不是军队——而是国家。你们所有人都是我们国家投入这场战斗的一部分，体现在研发、列装并把能力交到我们的……手中。”
items.zhFull:
代顿，俄亥俄州（AFLCMC）——“你们是战斗的一部分，”美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）司令 Lt. Gen. 贾森·沃里斯（Jason Voorheis）本周早些时候在俄亥俄国防与航空航天论坛上对与会者说。“戴尔·怀特将军（Dale White）[五角大楼关键重大武器系统主管]喜欢说，军队不会开战——国家才会开战。你们所有人都是我国为这场战斗所贡献力量的一部分，无论是开发、列装，还是把能力交到我们的作战人员手中。”

沃里斯作为题为“来自腹地的力量投射”的专题讨论小组成员发言。与他同台的有 Brig. Gen. 蒂莫西·赫尔弗里希（Timothy Helfrich），AFLCMC 战斗机与先进飞机组合采办执行官（PAE），以及国防工业专业人士 TK·库比特（TK Kubit）和安东尼·凯恩（Anthony Cain）。JobsOhio 的 JP·诺西夫（JP Nauseef）主持了讨论。该论坛由代顿发展联盟主办。

论坛于2026年9月21日在莱特州立大学举行，凸显了空军现代化优先事项与俄亥俄国防生态系统之间的战略协同。

采办速度与敏捷性

俄亥俄国防生态系统

劳动力与人才发展

沃里斯在开场致辞中解释说，空军采办队伍正在转变，更早接受风险，积极采用商业技术和开放任务系统，并赋予项目团队作出推动项目前进的决策的权力。

沃里斯和赫尔弗里希都指出，Wright-Patt 以及整个中心的采办团队正从针对特定平台的“烟囱式”模式转向，专注于先进飞机更广泛的一体化能力。这些团队还在平衡当前密集的机队现代化与未来系统开发，从单个平台升级转向一体化的“系统之系统”方法。

“我认为采办转型真正重要的部分之一，是理念的转变，以及把交付已列装能力作为我们最重要的优先事项和节奏牵引，而其他一切——包括我们赋予PAE的权限——都是为了实现这一目标，”沃海斯（Voorheis）指出。

赫尔弗里希（Helfrich）的“战斗机与先进飞机”组合包括A-10、F-15、F-16、F-22，以及FQ-42、FQ-44和其他协同作战飞机。

美国空军研究实验室（AFRL）也总部设在赖特-帕特森（Wright-Patt）。赫尔弗里希盛赞AFRL在开放架构方面引领了关键进展，并将协同作战飞机（CCA）项目的发展归功于AFRL。

“没有美国空军研究实验室，就不会有CCA，”赫尔弗里希解释道。“AFRL对FQ-42‘复仇’和FQ-44‘狂怒’都投入了大量资金。由于CCA的软件是单独销售的，任务自主性工作始于AFRL。他们确实是组建首个联盟来构建自主政府参考架构（A-GRA）的一方。这已成为一个庞大的项目，而这一切都得益于AFRL的投资。”

对沃海斯和赫尔弗里希而言，劳动力和配套基础设施仍是首要关切。赫尔弗里希敦促在场教育工作者对军事工程和软件开发课程进行现代化改革。两位发言人都指出，赖特-帕特森周边地区缺乏实体国防基础设施，尤其是用于高级别机密工作的设施。

除实体设施限制外，招聘仍是一项挑战。美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）目前有超过1,700个职位空缺，其中一半以上位于赖特-帕特森。大多数空缺职位属于工程和后勤等技术领域。合同签订和项目管理等业务领域也有许多空缺。

“我们需要在从大学以及产业界招聘方面获得帮助，既包括国防产业，也包括非国防产业，”沃海斯解释道。“你不需要带着丰富的航空航天经验入职。我们真正需要的是才华出众、积极进取、善于批判性思考的人。”

此次小组讨论标志着Lt. Gen.沃海斯自上月底就任指挥官以来，首次公开谈及他领导AFLCMC的职责。
zhParas: 代顿，俄亥俄州（AFLCMC）——“你们是战斗的一部分，”美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）司令 Lt. Gen. 贾森·沃里斯（Jason Voorheis）本周早些时候在俄亥俄国防与航空航天论坛上对与会者说。“戴尔·怀特将军（Dale White）[五角大楼关键重大武器系统主管]喜欢说，军队不会开战——国家才会开战。你们所有人都是我国为这场战斗所贡献力量的一部分，无论是开发、列装，还是把能力交到我们的作战人员手中。”

沃里斯作为题为“来自腹地的力量投射”的专题讨论小组成员发言。与他同台的有 Brig. Gen. 蒂莫西·赫尔弗里希（Timothy Helfrich），AFLCMC 战斗机与先进飞机组合采办执行官（PAE），以及国防工业专业人士 TK·库比特（TK Kubit）和安东尼·凯恩（Anthony Cain）。JobsOhio 的 JP·诺西夫（JP Nauseef）主持了讨论。该论坛由代顿发展联盟主办。
论坛于2026年9月21日在莱特州立大学举行，凸显了空军现代化优先事项与俄亥俄国防生态系统之间的战略协同。
沃里斯在开场致辞中解释说，空军采办队伍正在转变，更早接受风险，积极采用商业技术和开放任务系统，并赋予项目团队作出推动项目前进的决策的权力。
沃里斯和赫尔弗里希都指出，Wright-Patt 以及整个中心的采办团队正从针对特定平台的“烟囱式”模式转向，专注于先进飞机更广泛的一体化能力。这些团队还在平衡当前密集的机队现代化与未来系统开发，从单个平台升级转向一体化的“系统之系统”方法。
“我认为采办转型真正重要的部分之一，是理念的转变，以及把交付已列装能力作为我们最重要的优先事项和节奏牵引，而其他一切——包括我们赋予PAE的权限——都是为了实现这一目标，”沃海斯（Voorheis）指出。
赫尔弗里希（Helfrich）的“战斗机与先进飞机”组合包括A-10、F-15、F-16、F-22，以及FQ-42、FQ-44和其他协同作战飞机。
美国空军研究实验室（AFRL）也总部设在赖特-帕特森（Wright-Patt）。赫尔弗里希盛赞AFRL在开放架构方面引领了关键进展，并将协同作战飞机（CCA）项目的发展归功于AFRL。
“没有美国空军研究实验室，就不会有CCA，”赫尔弗里希解释道。“AFRL对FQ-42‘复仇’和FQ-44‘狂怒’都投入了大量资金。由于CCA的软件是单独销售的，任务自主性工作始于AFRL。他们确实是组建首个联盟来构建自主政府参考架构（A-GRA）的一方。这已成为一个庞大的项目，而这一切都得益于AFRL的投资。”
对沃海斯和赫尔弗里希而言，劳动力和配套基础设施仍是首要关切。赫尔弗里希敦促在场教育工作者对军事工程和软件开发课程进行现代化改革。两位发言人都指出，赖特-帕特森周边地区缺乏实体国防基础设施，尤其是用于高级别机密工作的设施。
除实体设施限制外，招聘仍是一项挑战。美国空军生命周期管理中心（AFLCMC）目前有超过1,700个职位空缺，其中一半以上位于赖特-帕特森。大多数空缺职位属于工程和后勤等技术领域。合同签订和项目管理等业务领域也有许多空缺。
“我们需要在从大学以及产业界招聘方面获得帮助，既包括国防产业，也包括非国防产业，”沃海斯解释道。“你不需要带着丰富的航空航天经验入职。我们真正需要的是才华出众、积极进取、善于批判性思考的人。”
此次小组讨论标志着Lt. Gen.沃海斯自上月底就任指挥官以来，首次公开谈及他领导AFLCMC的职责。
